MR. DISRAELI-THE COMING MAN.

READING Mr. DISBA.ELIIE speech is a trying
task, Listening to it, except to the most
stupid and zealous Conservative, cannot have
been otherwise than a trial of temper. It was
neither instructive nor amusing. It lacked as
much the weight of solid statesmanlike argu-
ment as it did the more fanciful graces of
a refined oratorical display. It was as poor in
thought as it was tawdry in ornament, and as
the exposition of the future policy of a great
politioal• patty it was rambling• and incon-
clusive. It contained 'a novelty or two,
such as the assurance that the poverty of the
Dorsetshire labourers was the result of
smuggling 'in bygone days, which is as
curious a discovery in its way as that pre-
viously made by the Hon. Gentleman as to the
proximity of the Atlantic being the cause of
Irish discontent.

We all know that Mr. DISRAELI is very
clever; nobody has doubted this since he
first brought himself under the notice of the
British people; but when be is placed before
the public so prominently, and after such elabo-
rate preparations as were made for his visit
to Lancashire, we have a right to look
for something better than chaff and badinage,
now gracefully and dexterously blown into the
faces of Mr. GLADSTONE and his eolleagues,
and then blindingly puffed into the eyes of Sir
CHARLES DUKE and his Republican followers.
Nor is abuse of any kind worth much on such
an occasion as this. Our great Conservative
orator has no doubt many followers who could
without much previous preparation undertake
this part of the work .and. execute it in a very
satisfactory manner. It was not becoming
either that he should have scolded those who
visited South Warwiokshire in reference
to the labourers' strike. " Extraneous "in their
"Ideas" and " influences" they may be; that
is, if Englishmen with English ideas can fairly
be regarded as " extraneous " in England.
But be this as it may, such a snub should not
have been administered by Mr. DISRAELI, who
was himself at the moment an " extraneous "
influence in Laneashire, and in regard to the
country generally, very much more "
neous " than any of the gentlemen to whom
he administered his rebuke.
We have a right to thank him, however,
for the large concession made in his artistic
round-about way,—" I do not say for a moment
that there is not room for more improvement
in the condition of all classes of the labouring
population of this country." Lest, however,
this should be taken with too large a meaning,
a previous qualifioation was provided—" 1

DISRAELI'S eyes. And that "mileage", which

hearers laughed at, is no doubt a republican
extravagance. Then again, the cheap honours
of '1 string" and" ribbon" which our great men
are satisfied with, instead of hard cash 'as
in America, is greatly in our favour, if we are
to believe all he told his Conservative friends ;
Only it was hardly fair on his part 'to 'conceal

of the Exchequer out of pleee, he himself is
in the annual receipt of something like a
couple of thousands sterling—a kind of sole-
tium not given in the United States to broken-
kneed financiers.

But why should we take this political
Roam, and "out him out in little stars," in-
stead of seeking to get at him in his full efful-
gence? Why should we carp at the playful
attitudinising of a strolling politician at
Eastertide, instead of trying to get at the
completeness of his moaning—the serious pur-
pose of his prolonged utterance? This is pre-
cisely what puzzles us. We have tried it, and
failed. He told us what his policy was not.
It was not to despoil churches, or plunder
landlords. It was not to attack or menace
every interest and. every institution. We can
believe this as perfectly true of the Hon. Gen-
tleman and his party just as every fair-minded
man in the country must believe it to be abso-
lutely false when applied to his political oppo-
nents, and shamefully disingenuous and
demagogic when addressed to such a crowd as
his Lancashire audience.

It is not however what his policy is not, but
what it is, we are interested in knowing; and
this, at the outset of his speech, he promised
he would give US to understand. These are
his words—" Our opponents assure us that

the Conservative party have no political pro-
gramme ; and, therefore, they must look with
much satisfaction to one whom you honour
to-night, by considering as a leader and repre-
sentative of your opinions, when he comes
forward at your invitation, to express to you
what that programme is.''
Just so; we did feel very grateful; but our
gratitude was premature, for at the end of
this lengthy and flashy speech we felt as far
as ever from a knowledge of the promised
programme. It is not to be found either in
detached fragments, or as a whole. It is not to
be got at as direct statement, or by inference.
It eludes the reader whether he disjoints
the sentences, or ingeniously splices them
together. It is as if he had canght up
his audience as grown people used to catch
up children by the chin and the back
of the head, to "show them London," and
after giving them a shake, set them on their
feet again in a state of painful wonderment.
He tells nothing that was not known before;
explains nothing that needs explanation. We
simply get to understand. that we shall have
a severe struggle at the next election, that

,Conservative than they
are Liberal as instruments of reform. What
people wish Mr. DISRA.ELI to tell them is what
he is prepared to do if they help to put him
in Mr. GLADSTONE'S place; but that he seems
determined to kee pto himself. People want
to find out what promise there is in him as a
statesman; but the oracle refuses to give an
intelligible response. The country is angry
with Mr. GLADSTONE and his colleagues be-
cause they are occasionally cowardly and
crooked; because thoy refuse to satisfy the re-
quirements of the nation in a soundly liberal
and progressive spirit. But this is no reason
why Liberal men should throw themselves
into the arms of Mr. Dish..tur. It is a rea-

articles.title: THE. MUTINY DILL.
articles.text:
THE. MUTINY DILL.

I SEE from Messrs. HA.NSAILD'S reports, that
on April 4th the Mutiny, Bill was" considered
in Committee and reported without amend-
ment, and ordered to be read a third time.".
This is so continually the case, year *after
year, that people have, to a great extent,
become ignorant of what is really contained
in the Mutiny Bill. There is one clause in
particular which I desire to bring before you
and your readers. The clause to which I
refer is as follows :
"No soldier shall be liable for not supporting
or maintaining, or for not having .supported or
, maintained, or for leaving or baying left charge-
able to any parish, township, or place, or to the
common fund of any union, any relation or child
which such soldier or person might, if not in
her Majesty's service, be compelled by law to
relieve or maintain; or for neglecting to pay to
the mother of any bastard child, or to any person
who May have been appointed to have tho custody
of such child, any stun to be psid in pursuance of
an order in that behalf."
It needs but little comment of mine to
point out the iinthorality and injustice of this
dause, which is thus re-enacted year after
year, granting free licence in vice to soldiers,
while at the same time specifically. and by
Act of Parliament depriving their unfortunate
victims of every hope of redress. It is little
enough redress that the law ever, under any
circumstances, gives to a woman who has
been betrayed. That subject forms one of the
greatest blots in our laws.; but it is a terrible
injustice to women when the law, insufficient
as it is, is thus year by year entirely abrogated
for a certain class of men. The evil effects
resulting from this clause are well known by
those who have come in contact with the misery
which is always left behind in the track, of
any set of troops, as it passes from place to
place; misery for which Parliament thus care-
fully year by year provides that there shall
be no redress. But the evils of the clause
will become of a more extended nature when
the new regulations as to the localisation of
the army come into effect; and. I much hope,
therefore, to see some publicity given to the
fact that such a clause exists., as in general
there is great ignorance, about it, except
amongst those who have suffered from it, or
have been ruined by it. Can it be wondered
at that women should dread the appreach of

troops, or that, for the sake of the weaker and
morelignorant of their own sex, the women
who inhabit the new districts marked out for
the " localisation" of bodies of troops, should
be looking forward with uneasiness and dread?
Bad legislation has two ovil effects; it has
direct and indirect evil effects. I pointed out
in an article lately in the Bn-lIINE, the
indirect evil of the system of minute police
supervision, which sets the people and those
who should naturally be their guardians and
protectors in a state of forced, unnatural, and
dangerous antagonism to one another. In
precisely the same way the clause which I have
referred to in the Mutiny Bill, and similar

evil legislation of the same character, tends to
make the army an object of dread and horror
to right-minded persons, and. to those who
desire to see the progress of morality and of
equal and just laws; and those, who, under a
good system, ought to be our beneficent pro-
tectors, become under such evil laws the
curse and degradation of our country, and a
canker which eats into the heart of our
'national well-being.

Very similar to this clause in the Mutiny
Bill is a clause in the order recently issued by
Superintendent llAnnts to the metropolitan
police, where he tells the police "to avoid any
interference with soldiers for drunkenness or
irregularities."
Now I would just ask your readers for
moment to compare this order, and to com-
pare the clause ihich I have just quoted from
the Mutiny Bill, with the infamous spy system
so elaborately organised under the Contagious
Diseases Acts, among the very same body of
policemen, with regard to the victims who are
first infected by these "irregularities,' and who
are then legally tortured to fit them for
further abominable use.s. This comparison
will show us how thoroughly some of our
legislators and officials are inibued with the
sentiment expressed by the Royal Commission,
that what is a sin and to be punished in a
woman is no sin and is not to be punished in a

man.
This infamous doctrine, from which spring,
so Many of the evils of social life, is nourished
and turned into practice by the existence of
laws which treat Men and women differently,
Mr. Baucn'S Bill for the prevention of Con-
tagious Diseases is precisely such an ovil la*.
He proposes to punish women with the utmost
rigour, to institute a system by which every
woman. accused Of any misdemeanour or
crime will have always at the same time to
rebut two charges, and be subject at the
caprice of a magistrate to a double punish-
ment, namely the punishment for her crime,
and nine months in addition if she prove to be
diseased, accompanied by ' enforced surgical
violation. It is a monstrous thing that a
woman should always have this hanging over
' her head, but it is especially monstrous, when
we find that, from beginning to end of the
Bill, there is not one word said about men.
Surely, sir, the education of such unequal
laws as these is calculated to undermine the
morality of our nittion, and to serve the very
end which Mr. tuncE, in the House • of
Commons, openly declared was his aim,
namely, to educate the nation to accepting the
Contagious Diseases Ads throughout the
length and breadth of the laud. .
But, sir, it is . not only for the sake el
Women that I appeal against unequal laws;
but no less for the sake of Men also. What is
a, yOung man educated under such laws as
these to think? What is he to think when
he fin& the law lets him g freo from even the
smallest pecuniary inconvenience, while it
,pimishos women, and , tortures
.them ..into fit
machines' for his vices? What, but that there
is no • blame attaching, to him, and that it is
the natural duty of the State to supply food
for his immoralities?
I lately perused a report on the snbject of
recruiting„ `drawn up for Mr. CA.RDWELL by
Major CLEMENT EDWARDS, Where it VMS ad-
vised that all clergymen and ministers of
various denominations should use their influ-
ence in persuading the young men of. their
neighbourhood to enlist, by bringing before
them fie advantages which they would have
Over civilians in a vast variety of ways, and
particularly in the experience of life and of
the world to be obtained in the army, When
I read the clause in the Mutiny Bill, and see
that this experience of life, and these advan-
tages include unlimited licence and _liberty to
abuse and seduce 'women, and to desert their
children, legitimate and illegitimate, free
from. all restraint, I am struck with horror
at the proposal that such "advantages" should
hie advocated from any Christian pulpit. And
when we see advertisements for young men
for the army, wn cannot shut our eyes to the
fact that among the "inducements" held out
in the name of the QUERN, is immunity in
vice, as well past as future, and leave to break
with impunity every previous tie. You will
see, then, that in. the. Mutiny Act the State

directly and impiously teaches and encourages
men to escape from the most sacred duty on
earth, the duty which a father owes to his own
flesh and. blood. This is the most suicidal
polioy,which a state could adopt, inasmuch as
it, in the most direct and explicit manner, and.
by positive enuctment, hits at the very root Qf
all that binds a nation together. Captain
BROWNE, of Woolwich, attributes a great part
of the immorality of the army to this clause in
the .Itutiny Bill. He says, in his evidence
given before the late‘B.eyal Commission—
"By that clause any civilian can at any time
throw over the claims of his wife and family by
enlisting, and any soldier married, whether with
or without leave, can repudiate his wife at any
moment by,virtuo of that .clause; and it is done
frequently."
In conclusion, Sir, I wish your readers to
observe that the effect of such laws as this is
becoming daily of more vital importance to the
nation, when we remember that the increase
of shorter service in the army is exposing snore
men to the evil influence of these laws. The
more extended " localisation," also, of the
army will soon expose many more districts to
the evil teaching which this unbridling of the
passions of men confers. And it is easy to
unbridle men's passions, but very difficult to
bridle them again.

We can only succe;sfally contend against
these infamous laws, and avoid the terrible re-
sults to which their extension is leading, by a
vigilant and determined attitude, and by the
combined resolution to sweep the evil princi-
ples completely out of our legislation.
. SA.IIO STUIRT, M.A.,
Fellow and Assistant Tutor of Trinity
College, Cambridge.

QUESTIONS BY I POSITIVIST.

EIGHTH, QUESTION.-Will• not 44 form of
socialism by its necessary rules and regulations
to produce order and co-operation interfere
with the free play of individuality, which is so
dear to modern civilisation and modern ideas
of freedom? And is it at all likely that the
working classes, of all classes, will submit to
this interference with their individual free-
dom? The interference with men's freedom in
the present state of society is not like that
necessary for systematic socialism.
ANSWEIL—The "necessary rules and regu-
lations" of the co-operative social system will
result from the knowledge of the causes of evil
and of good to man, and from the character of
enlightened goodness consequent upon this
knowledge. The leading objects of these rules
and regulations were stated in the 13nt-lIIRE

tutional requirements of the new system;"
and it is not at all likely that "the working

And it must be evident upon due considera-

of the new system, will be organised under the
guidance of the enlightened desire to promote
the well-being and happiness of erery indivi-

When men have acquired the character of
enlightened goodness, everyone will be an en-
lightened "law to himsolf"—everyone, will be
an enlightened and willing observer of that

While men arc educated as they have

been universal, and are of necessity subjected

order in the existing system, their personal
liberty of action, their freedom to do as they

would like to do, is inevitably very much in-

terfered with. And in the present system how
muoh is the frredom of all curtailed by em-
ployments which are irksome to them, by
deficiency, of pecuniary means, by an ignorant
and stultified public opinion, by intelleetual

and moral defects in themselves which cause

hem to have unwise and ill-regulated desires

new system will provide the means to eman-

tuid they will have, the means to enjok "the

,goodness.

In Mr, OWEN'S " Outline" of the now
tern, an enumeration is given of the chief

which will ultimately be secured for all," when
men have acquired the improved intellectual
and moral character of the new system, and
have formed,theksocial arrangements in accord-
ance with this character. I will state them

1. Tho possession of a good orgauisitioo,

2. The power to procure at pleasuee what-

3. The best attainable education, from

4. The inclination and means to promote

5. The inclination and means to increase

q. The power to enjoy.the best slciety ; ani

10. The utmost individual freedom of

11. To have perfect trathfulnes4 ; and t

olone'ean produce.

—through the acquirement of the knowledge

articles.title: HENRY TRAVIS.
articles.text:
HENRY TRAVIS.

THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT.
THERE was once a eunuch who was called to
the throne of Khorassan, and who was a

sternly virtuous being. He had such a horror
of the deadly sin of unehastity that he
punished men and women wholesale whenever
he detected them erring in their loves. Not
satisfied with severely punishing the offenders
themselves, he included their innocent fami-
lies in his vengeance. When he caught a man
sinning he was of course punished, sometimes
by torture and mutilation, sometimes by
death. If the man were unmarried, the
vengeance of the King ended with the sinner,
but it the sinner had a wife and children the
latter were include d in the punishment. The King
would cut off the nose of the man and other-
wise grievously mutilate him. He would then
put the innocent wife to slow torture for
months and sometimes for years; he would at
times put out one or both of her eyes, disfigure
her fate, and curse her with feeble health. He
then put to death her poor children by slow and
lingering tortures, or would disfigure them.
Indeed, nothing seemed too severe as a punish-
ment to the incontinent or to the relations of
the incontinent. The King thus pursued his
course of repression until a large proportion of
Ms subjects were maimed, disfigured, or other-
wise injured; andlet strange to say, the sin
of unchastity flourished as much as over, but
it was driven into' earners ; there were more
secret frail ones, more violations, more unname-
able offences.

At last an ol.d Derviso came to the
court of the beardless monarch and remon-
strated with. him. " Oh, King SYPHILIS,"
said he, "punish thy subjects as thou wilt,
thou canst never extirpate the passions
which GOD has given .us, except by extir.
pitting the human race, even as thy progeny
has been checked. Fight nob against human
nature, but aid the good. impulses within it.
Make marriage easier by making life eager, but
above all things endeavour to remove disease
from both innocent and guilty, for the guilt of
the latter cannot be measured by thee. It is

wrong to indulge the natural passions irregu-
larly, it is wrong to eat too much, but it
would be cruel to torture and kill the glutton
end his relatives for an occasional excess.
Lying and slandering are vrorse crimes than
incontinence, and yet death and mutila-
lation would be deemed severe punishments for
snob crimes as these."
I venture to recommend the above parable
' to those of your readers who haft) so violently
opposed the Contagious Diseases Bill, but as I
am unable fully to treat the matter in the guise
of a story, I drop this form of address and
proceed to speak plainly.'
well remember as a medical stndent, a
• young prostitute coming to the hospital to
be voluntarily examined, as she suspected there
was f 4 something theanatter " with her. She
was pronounced infected, on which she started.
up in a fury, used. the mOse.atrocions language,
cursed the whole male sex, aniswore she would
,revenge herself on every man si.e could lure to
her bed. She went forth, armed w:th a poisoned
nagger, determined to stab right aryl left, and
glorying in the liberty of the British prostitute.
It may be said that no one need be otabbed
bat those who entered her house. Hold there;
(Jon alone knows how many fell beneath the
poisoned dagger of that furious prostitute ;
nct only
men, but innocent women, and chit-
(l“,in. Let us suppose a case; a case, too, wbich I
have known in my own professional experience.
A. youth is Wranderipg about and meets this
WOMPI. She appeals to his passions (passions,
.the strength and nature of which can no
more, be understood by certain chaste and
.hysterically angry ladies than colours can be
appreciated by a blind man), the youth yields,
perhaps for the first time in his life, he is
infected, and after months. of suffering, re-
covers. Penitent and reformed, he determines
to marry. Ma dootor really thinks he may
safely do so, and lie unites himself forthwith
to a lovely, virtuous girl. But the disease is
lurking in his blood, the poison is mysteriously
conveyed to his offspring, the untimely fruit is
dead, but not before the child had infected the

young mother, We need not pursue the
gloomy subject further; we will draw a veil
over the horror, remorse, and disgrace flowing
from one sad act of incontinence. Suppose
that the furious prostitute had been compelled
to undergo what Mrs. JOSEPHINE BUTLER is
pleased to call "instrumental violation," the
very operation she voluntarily requested—an
operation any and every modest woman sub-
mits to voluntarily, to be healed when any
disease attacks that part of the body—suppose,

I say, that a notorious prostitute were forced,
for the good of the public, to undergo this
examination, why all this noise? In this
world so full of imperfections, we are con-

steady obliged to choose the lesser

of two evils. Which, then, is the
lesser the sowing broadeast disease

amongst guilty and innocent, or the " instru.
mental violation" of common prostitutes?
Prostitutes, by their very profession, put
themselves in the position of attacking society

with poison. To protect society is the supreme
duty of Government; therefore their persons
should be searched for the poison. If lam
suspected of harbouring stolen goods my
domicile may be violated by the police to
searoh for the same on a warrant being issued.
If I am under surveillance in consequence of
a life of crime, no warrant is necessary.
It is idle to talk of the injustice of treating
women so when men are not examined. The
moment there exist male prostitutes let the
law include them. .4'

The question as to the success or not of the
Acts is 'another matter. That question, and
the most important one, it is impossible to
determine in face of the ignorant clamour and
appeals to passion thathave arisen. As far as
I can judge had the disease been extirpated
there would be a cry for its restoration. The
majority of the agitators appear to me to be
less anxious for the maidenly modesty • of
prostitutes, than for the conservation of
syphilis, which they look upon as the Divine
retribution of vice.' Now I assert that the
disease in question is not the direct 'conse-
quence of sexual excess. The greatest sinners
in • this respect escape it altogether by certain
precautions. It is an accidental disease
usually, though not invariably propagated by
the act of procreation. Whole tribes of
innocent pastoral people have been- de-
cimated by this disease, perhaps .by the sin
of one or two persons. Burgeons frequently
catch it through their fingers. . A friend of
mine thus lost his life. Children are infected
by their parents, Wives by their husbands, and
children by wet nurses, and the latter by their
foster children.
Medical men have spoken with authority,`as.
was their duty, and have come in for un-
measured abuse in consequence. Now I may
observe that as a matter of pecuniary interest
it is obvious that the profession have as a rule
spoken against their interests. The more
disease the more money. I cannot conceive .a
more profitable patient than a sypliilitie one.
But these dootors-ha.ve spoken the truth, the
simple obvious truth, when they assert that
they are the best judges as to the means to be
employed to extirpate a disease from the com-
munity. No one • pretends that they are to
frame our laws even on sanitary matters, but
surely on matters of health and disease they
ought to be our chief advisers in public as
they are in private. It is marvellous how
cruelty of the most atrocious character
lurks in the breasts of good and gentle women,
of priests, and of pious persons, especially
towards.those guilty of vices to which these
immaculate people are not inclined. • I was
once connected with a hospital where we were
not allowed by the Board. to treat any venereal
disorders. We constantly violated this stand-
ing rule framed by Pharisees who indulged in

LONDON.
TUE SOCIETY OF IRON FOUNDERS.

The following is from Mr. Guile's Report just
issued:—

BROTHEIL MEMBERS,--•

In bringing under your notice the 213th
Monthly Report, we have pleasure in saying all
the Branch Reports were in to time according to
rule; and we are also glad to say that trade still
continues very good. There is a slight decrease
on the donation fund, all the scales combined, as
well as on tho sick benefit, as well as
there being an increase in the total number
of members, also an increase of £1,850 2s. 61d.
in the cash in hand during the month, the cash in
hand amounting at present to the poble sum of
£23,157 Bs. id., or a trifle over £2 4s. 51d. per
member. All thing are very cheering, and form
a striking contrast with what our position was a
very short time ago, and must give satisfaction to
every viell-wisher of the Society—then we '
scarcely know whore to turn to obtain help for our
suffering brethren. Our members were walking
about idle and could find no work; our invalid
members were patiently waiting for the time to
come when their claims on the accident fund could
be met. Some of our members had advanced
almost all they possessed to assist the strug-
gling and then apparently helpless Society
with strong faith that, by-and-,bye, the old ship
would right herself. A large number of the mem-
bers stood faithful to her, and have lived to see
the day when the storm has passed away, and now

it seems all sunshine—all accident claims met, all
loans paid off with interest, and a goodly sum in
hand. All these considerations give us cause for
joy, and renew our confidence in the power of
perseverance and unity. Our hope is, that during
the year we may have a continuance of good trade,
and that we may all so use it that at the end of
the year we may look back and find that it has
been a period of not only collective, but individual
prosperity, and to this end all our requirements
must be in reason. Let not our demands be ex-
travagant or exorbitant, nor such as it is impassi-
ble for employers to grant, or it may so happen
that we may kill the goose that laid the golden
eggs. Firmly let U 9 defend what we honestly
consider our right, and as earnestly protect and
carry out that which is the right pf others; an
by thus conducting ourselves and our business, we
shall earn the respect of all those whose esteem
is desirable.

BIRIAINGIIAM.
ARBITRATION IN TILE BUILDING TRADE.

On Thursday, a Board of Arbitration, presided
over by Mr. Rupert Kettle, County Court Judge
for Worcestershire, sat at the Grand Jury Room,
Moor-street, to consider a demand by the workmen
of the building trades for an alteration of the
rules agreed upon in 1867. The representatives
of the employers were—Messrs. W. Briggs, W.
13loore, J. Ilardwick, J. Garlick, C. Cotterill, and
J. Moffatt. On the prat of the workmen the
delegates were-711r. J. Loughton, secretary of the
General Union of Joiners; Mr. Lumen, secretary
of the Amalgamated Union of Carpenters and
Joiners; Mr. D. Btephen, for the labourers; Mr.

APRIL 13, 1872.

P. Garby, for the labourers; Mr. J. Davison,
secretrry of the Birmingham District of Plasterers;
Mr. J. Williams, secretary of the National AIM'

dation of Plasterers.
Mr. Briggs objected to the 'presence of Mr.
Williams on the Board, on the ground that he. was
not an operative plasterer. After some discussion,
the Abitrator decided on Mr. Williams remaining,
and observed that the men should be allowed
the utmost liberty of choice in the scle;:tiou of

their delegates.
After a long discussion, Mr. B:oore proposed, oil
the part of the employers, that the hours of 'work
should be 54 per week. Mr. Davidson, on the
part of the men, proposed that they be 53. The
vote was taken two or three times by the Arbi-
trator, and it resulted in six voting on the one
side, and one on the other.
The Arbitrator said he must decide the question,
and would do so; but he would first ask the dele-
gates of the workmen whether it was worth while
for the sake of an hour, to disturb the nine hours,
which was so general in the country.
Mr. Williams said the Arbitrator must remember
that the constituencies of some of the delegates
were very thick-skinned., (Laughter.)
The Arbitrator replied that a Board of Asbitra-
tion was a deliberate assembly, or it was nothing.
It was absurd to expect him to sit as umpire if

case. It must be understood that the whole ques-
tion was referred to him whether the time should
be 561/ hours 50/ hours, or something between.
On hearing this the representatives of the men
asked for an adjournment for half an hour.
On resuming, Mr. Williams said that having
consulted with his colleagues, they
had agreed to
await the Arbitrator's award as to 53 hours.
Mr. Loughton said he understood that the Arbi-
trator could give his decision at once.
The 4rbitrator said he could not do so, as there

hours being refused, he would consider what basis

The meeting was then adjourned, sine dic.

KETTERING.
THE BUILDING TRADES.
To the Editor of the BEE-Hirs.
Sin,---As my last letter to you went off from
our Committee in rather a pop-gun fashion,
I am tempted to try and explain more definite our
position. In the tirbt place we have for many
years been behind our neighbours in the matter of
wages, but feeling a difficulty in regulating the
various prices we decided to ask for the nine hours,
which would be a benefit to all of us, and get our
wages raised individually. Now we have been
refused our modest request on the grounds that it
has not become general in other places, with an
offer to take any man's case into consideration,

which we take to mean they will raise just a few
of the men they cannot do without. Sir, our main
objects are now to keep united altogether as we
are if possible, until we can get the branches
amalgamated, but at present there are only two
branches strong enough—viz., bricklayers and
carpenters; but I am afraid they have not the
men among them who would take the trouble
upon themselves. We also intend to try again
next spring for the nine hours; also to raise a fund
to provide some amount to members in case of
accident, the rest to be devoted to trade purposes;
and what the men seem eager to know from you,
Sir is, are we doing anything unlawful, and can
we get our rules registered, or get amalgamated to
you in a body as we are now? If it is not giving
you too much trouble, will you oblige us this week
as we want to keep faith and satisfy the men.
I hope we shall be able to get your paper shortly.
I uhall send you a Leicestershire paper with letters
from myself and others on this subject. Since
this question has been about, several of us have
been raised two shillings.—' am, yours &0.,

JAMES LONGLAND,
Secrotary of the Operative Builders' Society.
April 4th, 1872.

articles.title: SHEFFIELD. THE CABINET MAKERS.
articles.text:
SHEFFIELD.
THE CABINET MAKERS.

Stu,—In these days of struggling for right
amongst the working classes of this country, and
as a cheering contrast with the niggardly severity
and injustice -with which the wealthy landowners
and farmers are at this time treating their worthy
but down-trodden fellow-creatures, it may not be
uninteresting to your readers to be made ac-
quainted with the position to which we, the
cabinet makers of the well-known firm of Mess*.
W. Johnson and Son, of Sheffield, have attained.
As your readers are probably aware, we have
for a length of time been working fifty-one hours
for a week's work, but failing to see the advan-
tages to be derived from the reduction of hours
-without having the benefit of the long evenings,
our employers have kindly made arrangetnements
with their employes to commence work at 6.30,
and cease work at 6 o'clock in the afternoon, with
(of course) the usugl Saturday half-holiday ; thus
securing to their workmen every opportunity for
moral and mental, improvement, which, Sir, will
undoubtedly be productive of good feeling betwixt
masters and men, accompanied with renewed
energies for our daily occupation, as well as over
increasing intelli,ence, which must certainly be
beneficial to masters as well as men, and the
community at large.
I need scarcely add, Sir, that we, as workmen,
have received this concession with gratitude, it
being, we believe, the firs t concession to this ex-
tent made by any firm in England (in our busi-

nos).
Hoping, Sir, to speedily learn through your
columns that the short time movement, on the
long evening system, has greatly extended, and
much benefit derived therefrom,—l am, Sir, yours
respectfully, FIVE O'CLOCK.
P. 8.—1 am happy to say the short time (nine
hours) movement has become almost universal in
the Ironworks in Sheffield, and I believe in all
eases the day's work finishes at five o'clock.

articles.title: LANCASHIRE. THE COTTON SPINNERS.
articles.text:
LANCASHIRE.
THE COTTON SPINNERS.

To the Amalgamated Association of Operative
Cotton Spinners, Self-actor Minders, Twiners, and
Rovers of Lancashire and adjoining Counties. ,
FELLow-Woarrimr,—ln the numerous discus-
sions consequent upon the American cotton famine,
we have been frequently told that in all the great
cotton growing countries of the world (except
British India) the great drawback upon the pro-
duction of cotton is the scarcity of labour, and
that a more plentiful supply is not procurable
unless it be withdrawn from the production of
food. Now, as cotton is no longer the product of
slavery, it is not at all probable that it will soon,
if ever again, be produced at the same figure as
during the existence of that diabolical system.
The free labourer, whether black or white, will
naturally seek the beat market for what he has to
sell. Accordingly we find it stated that in 1869
a pound of cotton cost just as much to produce it,
as a pound of cheese, so that whatever may be the
cost of a pound of cheese, it is clear that if a pound
of cotton fill below that price, its production will
fall off, and the capital and hbour previously
engaged in raising it will seek other and more
profitable employment, so that the result will be
=ore food and less cotton, and vice versa. But
suppose capital to be withdrawn from the produc-
tion of food for the purpose of raising more and
cheaper cotton, how would such a change or viola-
tion of sound conimercial principle benefit us as
factory workers P If we produce less food we
raise its price, and depreciate the purchasing
power of our earnings. If by employing labour

formerly engaged in raising food, in growing
cotton (in India or anywhere else) we may for a
very short time secure a cheaper supply, and
possibly an advance in our money wages; but as
these wages will have been depreciated by the
higher price of food, it is clear that what is gain
on the one hand is loss on the other. From these
facts it seems plain that Great Britain possesses
facilities for the manufacture of more cotton goods
than she can find a constantly profitable market
for at the present price of cotton, and that its
price is seldom likely to fall much lower than at
present, therefore so far from further limiting the
supply of food by withdrawing labour from its
production when the market is barely supplied,
for the purpose of supplying more raw material for a
manufacture that is already overdone, our obvious
duty is to limit the operation of the latter to the
legitimate requirements of the market, say 54
hours per week by Act of Parliament. If there
be any reason in the world why such a regulation
should not be made in the present session of Par-
liament, We shall probably learn what it is on an
early day.
Richard Ainsworth, of Over Darwen, has been
overtaken by an accident from the machinery upon
which he was employed, which unhappily has re-
sulted in the loss of one of his hands. Unhappily
also (owing to circumstances over which he has no
control) the Over Dar wen district were not full
members of the Association at the time of the
occurrence, and consequently Mr. Ainsworth is
debarred from the benefit provided by its rules.
His fellow-members in the Over Darwen district
speak of him in the highest terms of commenda-
tion. They affirm that he has always been a good
unionist, that he is, in fact, one of those deserving
men never weary in the promotion of a good cause,
and that, therefore, he is fairly entitled to the
kindly sympathies of all good men. This being
the impression of the delegates, they avail them-
selves of this opportunity to recommend his ease to
the kindly consideration of the whole of the
districts of the Association. Signed,
THOMAS MAWDSLEY, General Secretary.
55, Store-street, Manchester, April 8, 1872.

MAIDSTONE.
TIIE BUILDERS' DISPUTE.

On Wednesday evening a hrge meeting o 1
carpenters and bricklayers of Maidstone was held at

the Sun Inn, High Street, to receive the report of
the conference between the , employers and the
deputation of workmen on the proposed alteration
of time and payment for work.

The meeting was called for eight o'cloz:k , but the
deputation of workmen, who met the employers at
half-past six the same evening at the Bell Hotel,
did not arrive at the Sun until nearly ten o'clock.
They then reported that no agreement as to the
men's requests had been arrived at. A long dis-
cussion ensued, in the course of which it appeared
that there were eleven employers and six workmen
at the conference, and Mr. J. Anscombe was in the
chair. The deputation, consisting of Messrs. Heard,
Vidler, and Connor (carpenters), and Messrs.
Arnies, Hunt, and Tomlin (bricklayers), explained
the desires of tho men, and the employers expressed
opinions to the effect that the workmen should
first get the time and wages of the otnlying dis-
tricts up to the Maidstone standard ere pressing
for an accession to their demands. Mailing,
Staplehurst, Tunbridge Wells, and other places in
the county were mentioned as being below the
Maidstone standard, and it was said that this state
of things placed the Maidstone builders at a dis-
advantage. The workmen took exception to those
statements, and appealed to tabular statements
furnished by . annual reports of the Operative
Bricklayers' Society, and the Amalgamated Society
of Carpenters and Joiners, to show that the state-
meats thus made were incorrect. A lengthy con-
versation then took plAce, and more than once high
words passed between the employers awl the work-
men. Eventually the employers intimated that
they would hold another meeting to consider the
statements of the men, and passed a resolution to
fors ard a reply to the deputation on or before
Saturday, April lath.
The workmen then adjourned until Saturday,
the lath, when they will again meet to receive the
employers' communication. It was intimated that
under no circumstances would the men depart
from their original resolution as to their requiring
the proposed changes to be made on the first
Monday in May.

LEEDS.
LEEDS ANT) DISTRICT TRADES COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Leeds and District
Trades' Council was held on Wednesday last at
Parker's Temperance Hotel. Thera was a good,
attendance of delegates repiesenting the following
trades :—Carpenters and joiners, coachtnakers.
ironfmnders, miners, cabinetmakers (two societies),
willeyera and fettlers, clothdressers, bruslunalters,

corn millers, tailors, engineers, masons, shoe-
makers, plasterers, skinners, and plumbers. Mr.
E. C. Denton occupied the chair.
The minutes of the previous meeting having
been confirmed, the secretary (Mr. Thomas
Plaokett) read the correspondence for the mouth,
which consisted of the replies of the borough and
county members to letters sent to them by him
asking them to support the Master and Servant
(Wages) Bill which have already been published;
also letters from the Trades' Union Congress (Par-
liamentary) Committee.
A deputation from the dyers of Leicester (who
are now out on strike for the nine hours' limit)
was introduced to the Council.

After hearing their statements, and examining
their credentials from the Leicester Trades' Council,
it was resolved—

"That this Council beg to recommend the case
of the dyers of Leicester to the various trade
societies of Leeds as one deserving of their sup-
port."
The memorial presented by the Trades' Union
Congress (Parliamentary) Committee to the Home
Secretary, praying for a repeal of the Criminal
Law Amendment Act, was then read.
After some discussion on the subject, in which
many delegates took part, it was resolved that the
Council use every possible means to• obtain a
repeal of this obnoxious Act, and call upon all
trades' unionists to use their influence with the
members of Parliament for the same object. It
being understood that the Bradford Trades' Coun-
cil intend holding a mass meeting at an early
date in favour of the repeal of the said Criminal
Law Amendment Act, it was resolved that the
Council take part in such mass meeting, and a
deputation was appointed for the purpose, the
secretary being instructed to communicate with the
Bradford Council on the subject as to the date;
and the Council also request that the various
trade societies will take part in it. Particulars
will be announced at a future date.
Subscriptions on behalf of the dyers of Leicester
will be thankfulLy received by Wni. Denning,
Talbot Inn, Applegate-street, Leicester.

articles.title: TUE FLAX TRADE STRIKE.
articles.text:
TUE FLAX TRADE STRIKE.

On Tuesday night, a crowded meeting of me-
chanics was held in the Peepla's Hall, Holbeck,
"to take into consideration the present position of
the flax operatives of Messrs. Marshall and Co."
The chairman of the meeting was Mr. David

White.
The following resolution was proposed by Mr.
Samuel. Woodhouse, seconded by Mr. Wrigley,
and supported by Mr. Luke Hope :
" That the iron trades in Leeds are determined
to stand by and support the flax operatives, if they
will only stand firm to the nine hours."
_ _ _

Mr. William Kendall said they had arrived at a
great crisis in the history of the flax trade. He
regretted that while the girls would remain firm,
the men would not. Speaking of the assistance
that had boon 'given to the strike, he said that
Barnsley had acted nobly. Though the men had
gone in, the girls would stand firm; and he be-
lieved that the operatives would still come out of
the struggle with honour to themselves and the
country. (Applause.)
Another working man made a statement, from
which it appeared that, in order to ascertain the
exact number of the persona who have resumed
work at Messrs. Marshall's, the men had watched
the live entrances to the mill, and they had seen

leave the premises 345 hands, about 2410 of whom
were said to be half tirners. The satne speaker
also stated that there were about 2,200 of Messrs.
Marshall's operatives still on strike.
A vote of thanks was passed to the chairman,
and as the meeting separated a collection was
made on behalf of the workpeople stilton strike.
The following circular has been issued :.--
FELLOW-IVOIMMEN.—It is evident that the side
of capital is very strong, and it is likely to be a
keen contest; therefore it behoves us as fellow-
workmen to rally round each other and be united,
in order to be successful.

Seeing that much confusion has occurred lately,
and that in consequence of some of the men of
other firms on the committee having deserted us,
particularly the over-lookers; we beg to say that
we could not pretend to pay the hands, as there
was no one to recognise them.

As to the rumours in the press that tbe 'flax strike
is at an end, we beg to state that it is false so far,
and at a meeting this day of the men of Marshall's,
Walker's, and Briggs's (Water, Lane), they have

pledged themselves to continue the struggle
through. It was intended at first to draw one or
two firms out, and by that means to win the
battle.

We pledge ourselves to keep firm until the nine
hour limit is obtained. We have not the least
doubt that if the men keep firm, the girls will do
the same.—We are, tte.,

SHEFFIELD.
THE PROPOSED NINE HOURS FACTORY ACT.

A conference was held on Monday at Sheffield
between Mr. Mundella, M.P., and the Joint
Executive Committee of Lancashire and Yorkshire
operatives for the purpose of discussing the pro-
visions of the bill to be introduced into Parliamettt
by the hon. gentleman for reducing the hours of
working for females and young persons in cotton
mills from 60 to 54 per week. Mr. Mundella laid
before the Committee 'a draft of the bill. It is
proposed that wherever the present Factory Act
reads "10b hours per day" it should be made to
read "9- hours a day;" and that "two o'clock
on Saturdays": should read "one o'clock on
Saturdays." Mr. Mundella stated that he hoped to
be able to introduce the bill either this or:next week.
He had secured a few staun la supporters of the
bill in the House, and he hrtd no doubt he sboul 1
be able to get some good names on the back of the
bill, irrespective of party. The Committee
thanked the hon. gentleman for the interest he
was taking in the movement.

BRISTOL.

TRE MASONS AND CARPENTERS.

ing of hours and advance of wages, and pledge

The farmers are willing to pay their labourers

would prevent the sudden strikes and sudden dis-
charges, and would be mutant) beneficial. The
farmers require that all such agreements should be
on stamped paper."

articles.title: LONDON RAILWAY SERVANTS.
articles.text:
LONDON RAILWAY SERVANTS.

On Tuesday evening a meeting was held at the
Winchester Arms, Southwark-street, at which Dr.
Baxter Langley presided, to take into considera-
tion the present position of. the various classes of
railway employs. The speakers showed the
necessity and desirability of having a reduction in
their hours of labour, and better remune-
ration for their labour, and to carry out these
advantages it was deemed necessary to form, them-
selves into an association to work amicably one with
another. it was urged that while other branches
of industry Shad their almsheuses, their super-
annuation funds, and other like itastitutions, rail-
way servants had no such advantage. They were
an important class of society, and numbered more
than any other trade or calling. In fact (one speaker
stated) that they were bigger than the British
Army. If any of the men complained to any of
the head officials they were soon made short work
of, and either got rid of altogether, or warned
to be satisfied with their lot or leave. The
only thing that managers looked after was secur-
ing good dividends for the shareholders.
The Chairman observed that the first step they
should take would be to become united among
tnemselves, and to effect this, the men upon the
different lines should see one another upon this
subject. lle had no doubt that if this were made
their basis to act upon they
,would soon obtain a
reduction in their working hours. There was a
difficulty he knew in the men meeting to state
their grievances, but this must be done Woo any
action could be taken. Per the moral, social, and
physical condition of the men, it was urged that
there should be a restriction in the hours of labour,
and that they should have one clear day in seven
for themselves. It would not suit the directors
themselves to have to work so many hours as the

guards, porters, &c.
After some farther conversation it was agreed
that definite action should be deferred till after the
next meeting had taken place, which is to he held
on Sunday evening next.
A. vote of thanks to Dr. Baxter Langley for
attending was passed, and the meeting separated.

THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT

CHARGE OF MOLESTATION.

Two girls named Fanny Wood and Elizabeth
Ann Westerman, and two boys calk(' Benjamin
Wood and William Hargraves, were summoned
before Mr. Bruce on Saturday morning, charged
by the Messrs. Marshall and Co., HoMeek, with
unlawfully molesting John Speight, one of their
overlookers, with a view to coerce the said John
Speight to quit his employment. The four
defendants were also charged with wilfully damag-
ing the windows and door of the complainant's
house by throwing stones. Mr. Braithwaite (Dibb,
Atkinson, and Braithwaite), appeared for the
Messrs. Marshall, and Mr. Granger defended. The
Messrs. Marshall opened their establishment on
Thursday last, and about 200 hands returned to
their work. Throughout the day there was much
noise, and a large crowd assembled outside at closing
time—six o'clock. Those inside could not leave
before seven or half-past, and when the complainant
(Speight) did get away he was followed home by slot
of boys, who hooted and " bashed " him. When
he got home he closed his door, but the crowd
began to thicken, and eventually they commenced
throwing stones. Speight's daughter and a
young man named John Atkinson were put out
of one of the back windows to go for a police-
man. Seven windows were broken and the deer
injured. Speight, his daughter, and John Atkin-
son proved conclusively that the four defendants
were prominently connected with the rioters,
who went away at about a quarter past nine
o'clock. The two girls had worked at Messrs.
Marshall's, but did not now, and all four were
stated to be in no way interested in the strike.
Speight said he was not aware that there were
any of Messrs. Marshall's workpeople in the
crowd,which assembled opposite his house. Mr.
Granger did not attempt to disprove the evidence
given, except as regards the girl Westerman.
Mr. Bruce, after hearing his evidence on this
point, said there could be no doubt all the four
were actors in this affair, and the only question
was one as to punishment. Mr. Braithwaite on
this remarked that the object of this prosecu-
tion was simply to bring home to the work-
peop'e that there was such an Act as this
MoLstation Act iu force, which would
stop proceedings of this kind. It would
satisfy the Messrs. Marshall now if Mr. Bruce
would suspend the sentence for a week, to see
what effect this prosecution would have upon the
operatives in the flax trade. If there should be no
further disturbance, Mr. Marshall would be glad

if the defendanis could be let off on entering into

their recognisances.
Mr. Granger said this was very kind a the
prosecutors; and Mr. Bruce also characterised the
proposal as a very handsome offer, for he should
have convicted in the case. The defendants must
understand that they owed their going out of
court not to him, but to the course taken by the
prosecutors. If it had been left to him he shoel3
certainly have sent them to prison, and for a
considerable time too, for although workpeople had
a perfect right to try to get the best terms they
could, yet they were not to use violence, intimida•
tion, or molestation to people who were willing to
work on the masters' terms. The conduct of these
defendants was the worse, inasmuch as they did
not appear to be inUrested in the strike a bit.
The defendants were now liberated for a week, and
to pay costs and damages fur the broken windows.

TU 11L .: TRADES UNIONISTS OF rue UNITED

GENTLEMBX,—For many years a large portion of
the community have suffered from a pernicious
system of Track. Frequent compleints have
reached -Parliament in refaence to it, which have
led to the appointment of Committees of Enquiry,
and latterly to a Royal Commission; the result of
which has been, the introduction of A Bill by the
Government as above-named.
The Bill in itself is essentially a-gool one; if it
became law as it now stands, there can bo no
doubt but that it would effectually destroy a
practice fraug'nt:with so many evils to the work-
men of this country.
The Rill also contains provisions for the prohibi-
ting of deductions from wages, a system under
which many and great evils have crept in, scarcely
leas injurious than Truck itself.
The Bill being a Government measure, and a
simple act of justice to the workman, protecting
him from oppression, we had hoped that it would
have passed without opposition; in this', however,
we have as usual been disappointed. Listening
to the appeals of those in the House who are sup-
porters of the system, and, therefore, opponents of
the Bill, the Home Secretary consented to a
Select Committee, That Committee, we fear, bears
a complexion unfavourable to anything like a
report which will settle fairly the questions dealt
with in the Bill.
Being appointed by the Congress held. at Not-
tingham to watch over this, and other measures in
the interests of the workman of this country, we
deem it our duty to sound to you this timely note
of alarm, and to urge upon you to take immediate
action to prevent the shelving of so reasonable a
Bill, or its mutilation in such a way as to destroy
its most important provisions. Permit us to point
out the course we deem most advisable for you to
take under the circumstances :

Ist. Wherever there is an organised society Nre
ask that society and its branches, at once to
convene meetings in support of the Bill, and to
write to their member or members in the borough
or county to give their uncompromising opposi-
tion to any delay, and an unqualified declaration
that any chuse permitting deductions will be
strenuously opposed.
2nd. Where no society exists, we call upon the
workmen in the special trades or districts to
assemble together and pass resolutions condemna-
tory of delay, or of any attempt on the part of
the Committee, or the House,
to weaken
most essential provisions of the Bill.
In a matter of such importance to all workmen,
we strongly advise that individual action should
be taken by constituents, for the purpoge of
;the
impressing on their members the necessity of
giving their best support to this long Promised
measure of reform.—We are, gentlernen, yours
truly,

articles.text:
THE AGRIOULTURAL LABOURERS'

STRIKE.

A meeting of the representatives of trades
societies was held on Tuesday evening at the
Sussex Hotel, T3ouverie-street, to devise means for
raising support for the agricultural labourers on
strike. The chair was taken by

Mr. W. Allan, of the Amalgamated Engineers'
Society, who said the council had thought it their

duty to convene a meeting, so that something
might be done towards the assistance of those who

were standing out in South Warwickshire so nobly
for an advance of wages. Everyone knew that for
years the agricultural laborers had been hold in worse
than slavery. The degradation and demoralisation
of their condition was heartrending, and if
unionists could be the means of assisting them out
of their present difficulty by helping them to
establish unions throughout the country, they
would be doing something not only to benefit the
agricultural labourers, but society at large. The
simple question at present was an advance of 3s.
per week, so that their wages might be 16s. After
all, what was 16s. a week to keep a wife and
family? (Hoar, hear.) The Iron Moulders had
already granted £2O; the Engineers had voted
£25, and, he believed, would agree to a levy of 2d.
from each member of the society, which would
realise something like £3OO, and be a good start.
(Cheers.)
Mr. Taylor, of Leamington, the hon. secretary
and treasurer of the Relief Committee of the
agricultural labourers now on strike, expressed the

thanks of the agriculturists for the sympathy
which had been shown to them in their strike.
The condition of the South Warwickshiro labourer,
though bad, was not so deplorable as in some other
parts of the kingdom. The average wage varied
from 108. to 135., but the condition of the labourers
was such as to call for a united effort to drag them

out of it. He gave an account of the origin of the
union at Wellesbourae, and tho difficulty of the
labourers in getting any conference with the
farmers. He had appealed for aid on his own

responsibility, and succeeded the first week in
getting £l4 for thorn, while the following week
sufficient was raised to pay most of them Os.. a
week. In three weeks £4OO was raised. The
men were in good spirits, and had managed by
migration to send away till who had not gone back
to work, except thirty or forty who were still on
the books. Sympathy was now being expressed
On all sides, and aid was flowing in apace. Though
the agricultural labourers might submit to arbitra-
tion as to the question of wages, they would not
submit to arbitration on the question of. unionism.
That they would never forego. Since the agita-
tion, wages in Stonelei,c,rh had been.raisod to 15s. a
week. Before the union, attempts to get a rise of
wages had been uniformly refused; though now
the farmers were saying that, if an increase of
wages had been asked for respectfully, they would
at once have granted it, 'rho fact was, that men
who, up to the present, bad been serfs and slaves,
had now aiserted their manhood, and would never
sink back into their previous condition.
. Mr. Guile, of the Iron Moulders' Society, moved
the following resolution :—" That this meeting,
representing many trade societies in London,
having heard the statement of Mr. Taylor, and
from information afforded by the daily papers,
resolve to use every means in our power for raising
funds to assist the
.agrieultural labourers in estab-
; lishing and maintaining a union, believing it to be
r the only lever by which they may he raised from

their deplorable condition to one in harmony with
the higher behests of a true and real civilisation."
Mr. Applegarth seconded the resolution.
Professor Beesly,.who was called upon by the
Chairman, said he had always looked forward with
great hope to something of this kind. Ile had
urged upon unionists in London that it was neces-
sary to try and excite the tendency to combination
amongst agricultural labourers, for, so long as
there was such a mass of unskilled and underpaid
labour in the agricultural districts, trying to raise
wages in towns was like trying to pour water into
a sieve. It must not be supposed that the tenant-
farmer was the only person besides the labourer
interested in this manner. The farmer, as a rule,

NUISANCES 7ACT.

•

On Monday, night avery large meeting of the
bakers of London was held in the Arundel'
Hall, Arundel-street, Strand, for the purpose
of obtaining exemption of the baking trade
from the operations of the Smoke Nuisances
Act, it having been found, as is alleged,
impossible for the trade to comply with its
requirements. Mr. J. Locke, M.P., occupied
tile chair, and he was supported by Mr.
Helms, Mr. W. H. Smith' M.P., Mr.
• W. M'Arthur, M.P., Mr. Harvey Lewis, M,P.,
Mr. Watney, M.P., &c. Several letters from
members of Parliament were read expressing
their inability to be present.
, The Chairman said it was about three years
since he had enjoyed. the honour of their
confidence. Ho had supported them because
he felt that the bakers of the metropolis ought
to have been left out of the Smoke Act. They
had not, however, been able to convince Mr.
Bruce, the Home Secretary, of that. He now
urged the bakers to go straight a head in
order to get themselves taken out of this
obnoxious Ad. .

Mr. Pringle moved the following resolution:
—" That this meeting, while admitting the
soundness, of the principle of the Smoke Nui-
sance Act, is of opinion that the biking trade
ought never to have been ineludel in its pro-
visions, inasmuch as it does not oonstitute
nuisance; and, secondly, that its conditions
are wholly dissimilar to those of all others
enumerated in the Act." Mr. Clark secontUri
the resolution. Mr. Helms, M.P., had always
felt that the baking trade was one that ought
to have been exempted from the Smoke Act.
To compare a small, oven of a bakehouse with
a large manufactory was preposterous, for on ,
comparing his own kitchen fire with the con-
sumption of a hundredweight of smoke in a
bakehouse, he found thatheconsumed as much
coal per day as they did. Their interests
were very safe in the hands of their represen-
tative in the House of Commons, Mr. Locke,
and he advised them to leavethe subject in his
hands. Mr. Watney, M.P., also addressed
the meeting.. He said he came there that
evening rather to hear what their grievances
were than to speak, and from what he had
heard he felt quite satisfied that it was quite
Impossible for them to comply with the Smoke
Nuisances Act—namely, to have a furnace so
as to consume its own smoke.
Mr. D waber moved a resolution calling
upon the Legislature to pass a Bill exempting
the baking trade from the Act, lie urged
that it was utterly impossible for bakers to
consume their own smoke, and it was a great
oppression that they should be subject to heavy
fines and imprisonment for non-compliance
with the Act. Mr. Ayrton, a baker, seconded
the resolution. Mr. M'Arthur, M,P, said
the arguments he had listened to that evening
from members of the baking trade were
most convincing, and he thought when they
were before Mr. Bruce he would be convinced
too that it was impossiote for the baking trade
to comply with the Act. Let them make
known their grievances to the House of Om-
inous, and he believed, those grievances
would be redressed. Mr. W. H. Smith,,
thought the bakers or London had shown they
had a real grievance which it was the duty
of Parliament to order an inquiry into. Mr.
Harvey Lewis, M.P" addressed the meeting
in support of the bakers' cause.
A. resolution was passed in support of the
Bill of Mr. Locke. The usual vote of thanks
;o the chairman, passed by acclamation,
;ermiaated the meeting.

LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.

ELECTION FOR WESTMINSTER •
FELLOW RATEPAYERS.—I have been invited again to
offer myself as a candidate for a seat at the London School
Board now vacant in the Westminster Division.
The Education Act has not been a success. It has led
to theological and denominational discussions, rather than
to united and intelligent efforts on behalf of National
Elucation. This has convinced me that all causes of dis-
sension should, as far as possible, be removed; and as
what is called the religious difficulty, is the math obstacle
in the way of practical educational work, I consider that
in any system of National Education, the State should
make provision solely for the secular instruction which
all children may receive in common; and that the respon-
sibility of the religious teaching of the young should be
thrown upon the various religious bodies.
The Act was passed to provide a good and useful secular
education for every boy and girl in England. No school
was to receive a farthing of public money unless conducted
on principles entirely unsectarian. The sending of child-
ren within certain ages to school was to be, by degrees at
least, compulsory; and, to this end, the schooling was to
be gratuitous in the case of those whose parents were
without means of paying for it.
Had the Act been carried out in this spirit by the Lon-
don School Board, the education of the children of working
men would not have been delayed, and the bitterness of
feeling now existing among religious parties would have
been narrowed.

As the question of the payment of Denominational Fees

is yet undecided by the Board, it is important for those
who are against this system to avail themselves of the
present vacancy, and secure the return of a candidate who

is against it.

It is agreed that, in a question concerning the interest
of the people, they should be represented by some men
from among themselves, and I, therefore, offer myself in a
district to which, by long residence, I belong, and for
which there is reason to believe that I should have been
elected in November, 1670, had proper arrangements been
made for taking the votes.
Relying on your support for ultimate success,
I am, yours obediently,

GEORGE POTTER.

PA.—Meetings, at which my views will be more fully
explained, will be held throughout the district previous to
the day of election, which is fixed for FRIDAY, APRIL
19th.

SATURDAY, APRIL 13, 1872.

THE PUBLIC HEALTH BILL.

Mn. DISRAELI has spent a week in Man-
chester and spoken three hours at a stretch
and all that remains impressed upon the minds
of those who heard him is, that he regards
the health of the people as the question now
most urgent. On such a point there needs be
no dispute. Important, however, as it may
be, the duty is one which can be attended to
without the postponement of any other subject
asking for consideration. It is curious, in the
meantime, to compare what he said at Man-
chester with what occurred in the House of
Commons on the evening of the day of his
return. There were two Health Bills, lie
stated, for both of which he should vote,
though he preferred Sir CHARLES ADDER
-
LET'S to Mr. STA-NSFELD'S. The former
he thinks admirable, because, while
consolidating at the same time that it
amends all existing sanitary Acts, it strictly
respects all existing local Acts. The Govern
ment Bill he deems very imperfect; especially
as not a consolidating measure, which lie
thinks most necessary.

This Bill, nevertheless, has been read the
second time by common consent, Mr. CDR..
RANCE withdrawing his proposal to send it to
a Select Committee, and Mr. FIELDEN, who
had threatened to move its rejection, with-
drawing his notice of motion. The latter
Member objects principally to putting local
authorities under central supervisiou, and to
attempting by the means proposed to cleanse
polluted rivers, means, in his opinion, inap-
plicable to narrow valleys, such as those of
West Yorkshire. Mr. WurrwELL also cau-
tioned the House against attempting too
much, more, on the one hand, than could be
accomplished; more, on the other, than is
called for. Driven from streams, manufacturers
might resort to lakes. In some recent eccperi-
'fleas a medical gentleman drank without
hesitation water containfng a mach larger in-
fusion of muriatic acid than is sent into a
stream by factories, and declared it not onlY
hoeilthy, hat pleasant. It is impossible,
moreover, to raise metals from mines without
pumping out the water and tinging the streams
in the neighbourhood. Mr. Dussnxits sug-
gested an intermediate body between the local
boards and the Central Board; as Sir. U.
SELWYN-IBBETSON recommended, a body of
public analysers; chosen, as Dr. Lunt advised;
by the Central, not the local authorities. Mr.
