The principal speech on the merits of the
Bill as a sanitary measure was that of Dr.
LYON PLAYFATR. He showed the necessities
arising from the rapid growth of towns, parti-
cularly of the larger size. With reference tø
London, he pointed out, that, while the three
millions .within
the metropolitan area were
provided for, the more than half a million only
just outside have no means of preserving or
purifying their area. It was therefore Wig° in
Mr. STANSFELD not to treat urban and non"
urban populations alike. He suggested, that
the officers called into existence should be
chosen from a space wide enough to make them
independent, and should pass an examination
, in the laws of health. He would not, how-
ever, pass by men on the spot of proved ability
-
With respect to running waters, he hoped that
we English would adopt the old law of Egypt,
"Thou shalt not pollute rivers." He reflected
' upon the selfishness of the Yorkshire and
Lancashire manufacturers who used the
whole streams on whose banks their factories
• were set down, and denied the plea of
necessity. When the late Lord DERBY carried
a Bill to prevent pollution of th 9
air by chemical works, impossibility was
pleaded; but the Act had not been long in
operation before ninety-seven per cent. of the
acids before given off into the atmosphere,
was condensed and saved to the great profit

of the manufacturers themselves. Insist upon
their keeping pure the waters, and they would
soon find means toll° it.
In fine, the most competent judge in Parlia-
ment, instead of regarding Mr. STANSFELD'S
Bill as "very imperfect," bestowed high and
emphatic commendation on it. For the first
time in our legislation, it deals positively
instead of permissively. Its principle is, that
all of us are entitled to breathe pure air, to
drink pure water, and to inhabit a
pure soil. Hero the natural philosopher
becomes a social prophet, and. assures us,
that this "very imperfect" Bill, as Mr.
Disumi affects to regard it, because it is
Ministerial and not Opposition, will, if faith-
fully worked, add eight years to all our lives.
"The great evil," says Dr. PLAXFAIR, "with
which the labouring classes have to contend
is, not the risk of dying, but the uncertainty
of living under the oppressive influence which
makes labour a pain, and very often life a
burden." With respect to the administrative
character and provisions of the Government
Bill, Sir C. ADDERLIM himself took a totally
different tone from his political and party
chief. It will spread throughout the country
the local management of local affairs.
Every district will have a responsible adminis-
tration. It will reduce, Sir CHARLES believes,
not increase rates; but, if not, the improve-
ment will well repay the cost. Thus sup-
ported, even by the author of the second
Bill, Mr. STANSFELD had little to do but
return thanks all round. As to an inter-
mediate authority, he should object if it
were administrative, but not if it were
simply sanitary. He announced his intention,
at the proper time, to bring forward a supple-
mentary estimate for a proper staff of
inspectors in addition to the present Poor-law
' inspectors, who would become sanitary in-
spectors under the Bill. 'With regard to
chemical tests, and the compulsory appoint-
ment of analysers, he has purposely left those
points open for the fullest discussion. London
was excluded from the Bill, leaving it to ask
for inclusion of its own accord. He did not
deny the importance of consolidation, but he
purposely avoided the inevitable length and
the contingent delay; but he readily agreed
that a short explanatory digest might be issued
by the Government for the use and guidance
of the sanitary Boards.

TIIE PRIESTS AND TUE PEOPLES.
THE Speech from the Throne at the opening
of the German Parliament referred to the pro-
gress of affairs in Alsace and Lorraine.. The
damage done by the war is disappearing. The
foundations of a German administration have
been laid, and the University of Strasburg
will be opened on the Ist of May. The Im-
perial Speech closed with stating that the
Emperor and King has succeeded in retaining
and strengthening the confidence of all
foreign States that the power acquired by Ger-
many through becoming united in one
Empire, is not only a safe bulwark for the
Fatherland, but likewise affords a strong
guarantee for the peace of Europe.
The Speech made no reference to the
quarrel with the Roman Catholic clergy, un-
less the new mode of inspecting schools be
included in the announced Bill regulating the
position of public functionaries. From other
sources, however, we learn that the Infalli-
Mists are losing ground, and the opposite
party gaining it. Thus, Rector GREUERT, one
of the latter sort, has held at Ingstenberg
first service, for which the Lutheran Church
was placed at his disposal, and all the Ca-
tholic soldiers of the garrison, with-
out exception, were present. In his
sermon he treated the POPE as a heretio,
who no longer belonged to the Church of
which he formerly was the head. With his
bishop he made a difference, proposing pea,eo..
ful co-operation in all things except the
imposed dogma. The attendance of civilians
was very large. The same thing is to happen
where the chaplain of a garrison does not
choose to submit to the Ultramontanes.
The relations between Prussia and Italy
point in the same direction. The POPE and his
partisans had flattered themselves, that Count
AuNn[ was their fast friend; but they now
denounee bint as a traitor. It was by special

direction of Prince BISMA.RCK that he was the

first foreigner to visit the CROWN PRINCE of

ITALY at the Quirinal Palace in Rome. Hence

the anger of the Papal faction throughout
Germany. It suits them both there and at
the Vatican to charge VICTOR EMMANUEL With

entering into special alliance with the Eat-
PEROR ; but of the pacific disposition of the

Italian Government there can be no rational
doubt. Between Germany and Italy no other
alliance is needed than the grounds afforded
them in common for distrusting, we do not
say dreading, the machinations of the priests.

What more -natural, under such circumstances,
than that Prince BTSIURCK should have in-

struoted Count ARNIU to inquire in what
manner the Italian Government mean to deal

with their implacable and unreasonable

adversaries?

The anti-Papal movement proceeds also in
France. The Archbishop of BORDE.B.IIX. has

provoked a spirit which will not be easily
allayed. The Abbe JUNQUA does not mean to be
passively extinguished. While awaiting trial
before the Assize Court of the Gironde, for

inciting to hatred and contempt of a religion
protected and recognised by the State, in a
newspaper article," he is carrying- the war
into the enemy's country. There are those who
think that he will not only be acquitted, but
prove to be the winning candidate at the next
elections. The population of Bordeaux is
divided into two camps, one for the ARCH-
BisuoP and the Prebendary who denounced
3'17-NU& for the sake of getting his stall in the
cathedral, and the other for the disgraced
priest and his friend the Abbe XIOULE. Twelve
vicars have sent in their adhesion to the
JUNQUA protest. The eloquent Father de-
clares for. "Anti-Popish evangelical doc-
trines," and is charged, he says, with a
politico - religious mission to the great
towns of France. He is severe "on
class vanity, worldly pride, and fossi-
lised creeds—the natural enemies of every
saving grace in the New Testament." He
speaks out on the social relations which JEsus
CppaisT came to establish between man and
man. "The Reformer of Galileo strove to
found the Christian Church upon a totally
different basis from that which the Popes
accepted as St. Peter's Rook. Ho blessed
liberty in humility; but he cursed arrogance,
ambition, avarice, hypocrisy, and tyranny.
He showed that all are children of the Uni-
versal FATHER, and therefore brethren. The
principle of Fraternity was not invented in
1789 in the Jacobins' Club, but in the car-
penter's shop of Nazareth. CHRIST loved the
people, and wept over the hard lot to which
they were born under Roman C.ESARS and
Judtcan tetrarchs, those spiritual ancestors of
the Popes and kings and governments which
support Rome and class despotism. CHRIST
suffered princes, but loved them not. His
FATHER'S kingdom was for the poor and needy,
the oppressed and wretched, for unfortunate
LAZARUS, and not for the effeminate and hard-
hearted DIVES. His love for the down-trod-
den comes out in every page of the New
Testament. His life was passed among the
poor. His consoling graces and healing vir-
tues were spent upon the poor; and his
greatest efforts were devoted to teaching the
poor to understand their rights and duties.
Though nineteen hundred years have passed
since He was a missionary to our planet, and
many Churches have been founded in His
name, the only truly Christian polity formally
accepted by a nation was proclaimed in 1789.
Republicans who turn their backs on Christi-
anity are grossly inconsistent. The Gospel
is the grandest formula of the Republican
faith. It places man in harmony with his
neighbour and with creation. If Frenchmen
accept it, they will build their Republic on
such a foundation that the gates of hell will
not prevail against it. JEsus CHRIST was a
genuine socialist; and he brought into the world
a great socialistic lover. He laid down the
true relations between cap ital and labour.
There is no social problem that we may not
solve by the earnest, humble, and frequent
study of His words."

articles.title: UNIVERSITY POR WALES.
articles.text:
A UNIVERSITY POR WALES.

DIE projected University for Wales makes
sure, but slow progress,. A. very fine new

building, the Castle House, Aberystwyth, was
for sale, and some patriotic Welshmen, favour-
able to the establishment of a University,
ventured to buy it. There being few com-
petitors, they got it for ten thousand pounds,
about an eighth of its cost. It contains fifty
large rooms, and a hundred and fifty bedrooms;
and is being fitted up with lecture room:;,
library, examination hall, dining hall, labora-
tory, museum, and common rooms; indeed,
with all the appliances of a University for seven
hundred students. It looks out over the sea,
and, being in a central town, is well adapted for
a National University. The chief difficulty
is want of funds. The Committee calculated
that, including the purchase-money of the
building, thirty thousand pounds would be
required, and as yet only seventeen thousand
have been raised. This, too, has come chiefly

from England; not that the Welsh people are
blind to the advantages of education. Where-
ever the landlord does not stop the movement,

the villages are all asking for School Boards;
and the demand for free education, apart from
all sectarian dogmas, is loud. But there are two
classes, the rich and tho poor, and their
religions are different. The landlords belong
to the Established Church ; the population
are almost exclusively Dissenters.

THE AGRICULTURAL STRIKES.

DISR.IELf s " jaunty " treatment o

the Warwickshire strike has provoked the
Daily News to send. their correspondent to
make a survey of the state of things upon
flughenden Manor. He found. matters:rather
worse than in and around Wellsbourne. We
must except Mr. DISRIELeS model cottages,
which appeared to be all that could be desired.
In general, however, the Buckinghamshire
labourer is in a case quite as hopeless as that

of the Warwiek.shire labourer; and. the Con-
servative leader will have to look at home.
To him and to others, we my recommend the
prompt example of Mr. CIIMILES SEELY, who
at a meeting with his tenantry, in the Isle of
Wight, stated that as the price of agricultural
labour was certain to rise, they should. at
once increase wages. Ile advised. an imme-
diate advance of three shillings per week, two
of which ho would contribute himself, if the
farmers would supply the third, which they
readily agreed to do.
In fact, it is high time that the farmers
generally looked about them. Even JOSEPH
Alton, the leader of the Midland movement, is
beginning to anticipate harvest with feelings
of uneasiness. Last year, labour was so scarce
that farmers were compelled. to pay almost any

price to get in their crops. The chances of
labour from Ireland lessen every year as men
settle into comfort there. If home labour fails
what is to be done? Machines cannot much'
alleviate the pressure. Their number islimited,
and crops cannot always wait until they go
round. Mr. Mlnx. Prunus, of Welcombe
Snitterfield, declares as a landlord that he does
not believe owners gat on an 'average 21 per
cent. on their oapital. If this is true, what
does it show? Either rents are very low, and
in spite of bad years, the farmer is doing well;
or if the rents are high the farming is poor.
Either he is hampered by restrictions, or he is
without secure and definite tenure, or else the
landlord neglects to provide for permanent
improvements. Anyhow, it is affirmed as a
fact, that the farming in War wiekshire is low
and miserable. It is useless to talk about the
poor per centage land yields so long as year to
year tenancy exists, and the landlord claims a
right to all improvements, thus forbidding his
tenant to put his capital out upon the soil.

articles.title: HOURS OF POLLING QUESTION
articles.text:
THE HOURS OF POLLING QUESTION

DIE Tories are terribly afraid of the conse-
quences of letting working men go to the poll
at hours when it would not interfere with their
day's work. Not the Tories only, but too
many of those who call themselves Liberals;
such Liberals, for example, as that former
Radical, the now Right Honourable WILLIAIt
EDWARD FORSTER. What, he affectedly cries
, out, what might not happen were voters
allowed to vote in the dark? Under the
Ballot, what difference can day or night
make? The truth is, that most men in full
employ could. not vote at all unless they had
the opportunity after the hours of work, After

six in the evening is the only time for them,
and two hours would be little enough, When-
ever this Government wants an excuse for
non-compliance with a reasonable request,
they say, wait a while until we have had ex-
perience. This specious excuse has been made
about the bad clauses in the Education Act;

it iS lOW repeated eonAerning the defects of
their Ballot Bill. We are indebted to Mr.
M'CuLLAGit Tonnulfs for 'shaming Mr. GLAD-
STONE and his influential colleague out of
their pretence. " What," he asked, " were
the Government afraid of? Afraid of the
dark? Why, the Ballot was darkness'. The
votes would be taken in a place where it
was the duty of the returning ()Meer to
provide lights. They would never be able to
I persuade the people out of doors that they
intended anything else but class legislation
unless they had the pell kept open at a time
when the working classes could vote." In the
end, Mr. FORSTEit promised to insert a clause
to meet the case. . The poll is to open at eight
in the morning, and close when the sun sets.
It is always to be open till four, and never
after eight, but is to shift between those hours,
as the days lengthen or shorten. This, if
faith be kept, will really extend the hours in
nine months of the year. But when dissolutions
occur at the dose of the year, there will be a
virtual disfranchisement of the working classes.
Of seven dissolutions during the present reign,

the last, however, was the only one that
happened in the autumn. Of four in the
previous reign, two wore in December; but
they were the only Christmas dissolutions
during the present century. The extension
to eight all the year round will be conceded
in the long run; yes, and must, for shorter
hours would act as a practical disfranchise-
ment.

articles.title: AGRICULTURIST IN 10'35.
articles.text:
THE AGRICULTURIST IN 10'35.

We extract from the Illustrated London
News some information which Mr. SIIIRLEY
Buooss.has condensed from Lord DlAcsur,A.Y's
celebrated chapter on the social condition of
England at the accession of JAMES the SECOND.
With the conclusion we entirely agree of
course, for the better the truth is understood,
the stronger becomes the case of the cultivator
of the soil :

"Into the subject of the Strike of Agricultural
Labourers this is not the place to enter. But, in
referring to Lord Macaulay's famous description
of the state of England in 1685, we come upon a
passage or two that may be interesting as illustra-
tive of the history of the labourer. The great
criterion (Nfacaulay observes) of the state of the
common people is the amount of their wages, and
as four-fifths of the common people were in the
seventeenth century employed in agriculture, it is
especially important to ascertain what were then
the wages of agricultural industry. The present
movement is in Warwickshire, and that happens
to be the county whieh the historiin selects as the
first district be examines. About the beginning
of 1685 the justices of Warwickshire, in the fixer-
case of a power intrusted to them by an Act of
Elizabeth, fixed, at their quarter sessions, a scale
of wages for the county, and notified that an
employer giving and a labourer taking more than
the authorised sum would be liable to punishment.
The wages of the common agricultural labourer,
from March to September were fixei at four
shillings a week, without food. From September
to March the sum was to be three and sixpence.
Warwickshire wages were about the average.
Those of Devonshire were ilire shillings, and those


on the border werevrobably low. In Suffolk the
labourer had five shillings in winter, six in sum-
mer. At this time the bricklayer, mason, or car-
penter earned probably half-a-crown a day. But
these figures, of course, tell nothing of the condi-
tion and comfort of the receiver of wages unless
we know what they would buy. Lord Macaulay
holds it as clear that, while the reward of labour
was in 1685 not more than half of what it was
when he wrote, there were few articles important
to the working man of which the price was not
more than half what it was when the history
was written. Beer was cheaper in the
old time, so was meat. In the cost
of wheat there had been little change. It vas
dear, and such bread as is now given in a work-
house was seldom seen oven on the trencher of a
shopkeeper or a yeoman. The nation lived on
rye, barley, and oats. The labourer would then
have paid snore than now for sugar, salt, coals,
candles, soap, shoes, stockings, and all articles of
clothing or bedding. Our enormous gain in com-
forts and luxuries, tharefore' has been enormously
shared by tho agriculturist. There is no reason
why he should not still try to improve his con-
dition, but let the truth be understood."

articles.title: OFFICIAL INCAPACITY. [COMMUNICATED.]
articles.text:
OFFICIAL INCAPACITY.
[COMMUNICATED.]

It is customary for political men who are
desirous of courting popularity, and of mem-
bers of Parliament who iwish to retain their
seats to attack the various items of national
expenditure, and to declaim in favour of re-
duced estimates for the great services of the
State. Such a course is almost sure to be
popular with the tax-paying classes of the
community, who groan under the heavy bur-
dens they are made to bear, and who are con-
stantly sighing for relief. The agitation of
ambitious candidates for public favour, and
the economical essays of those who, having
gained an entrance to the House of Commons,
wish to remain in possession, will, however,
have but little real effect whilst official in-
capacity reigns supreme in high places, and
men devoid of practical ability hold the purse
strings of the nation.

The only way that we see open for the
accomplishment of the object sought, lies in
the direction of a complete revision of the
mode of selecting and appointing the heads of
the various Governmental departments. At
present, official patronage and political influence
are the forces most active and most effectual in
supplying those heads, whilst talent and
practical knowledge are of no account what-
ever. The invariable practice in commercial
life whore everything depends upon the fitness
of the leading men for their posts, is to select
those leaders because they have proved them-
selves to have the requisite skill and judg.
ment for the due performance of their duties.
Having been found faithful over few things,
they are justly made rulers over many. Such
a course as by a natural law leads to good
results, and a judicious expenditure of capital
is closely associated with a wise and sensible
economy of that giant-like resource. A similar
principle ought to prevail in the appointment
of groat public officials who are invested with
the power of expending large sums of money
in their various departments, and who should
know how to expend those BUMS for the public
advantage. _ _ _

A certain test is now, it is true, applied in
order to gauge the qualifications of candidates
for subordinate offices in the public service;
but where is the value of subordinate talent
when official superiority, combined with official
incapacity, effectually keeps it in cheek, and
either snubs or neglects its possessors?
It would be an easy task to demonstrate the
faot that very many of the principal depart-
ments of the State are presided over by men
ignora. nt even of fhe rudimentary elements of
the work performed by their subordinates, and
who are perfectly innocent of any practical
knowledge of the duties they are supposed to
control. Is it at all probable, under such cir-
cumstances, that any legitimate or appreciable
reduction of the national expenditure can take
place?

It is idle to talk of saving money whilst
those who are entrusted with the power of
spending it are incapable of judging whether
it be rightly or Wrongly disbursed. If the
chief of a department be unacquainted with
the nature of the duties to be performed in it,
he is very likely—nay, almost certain—to be
"under the thumb" of some one else in that
department, and assuredly he cannot know
whether ho is using the "estimates" granted
for its maintenance with a proper amount of
discretion, or whether under the influences of

folly or cupidity he is not playing at "ducks
and drakes" with the earnings of the people
who are made to keep up the supplies. Official
incapacity is beyond a doubt responsible for
the sacrifice of much of the treasure of the
country. Would that it could be acquitted
of responsibility for the loss of lives, which are
of far more value to the country than the
contents of the national Exchequer. Until men
shall be put into positions of authority because
they are practical and meritorious, and not
because they have friends at court, the public
will have good cause to complain of extrava-
gance, and economy will be as completely out
of reach as is the Utopia of MOORE.

articles.title: CANON GIRDLESTONE AND THE WARWICKSHIRE STRIKE. , [Commurn CAI ED ;]
articles.text:
CANON GIRDLESTONE AND THE
WARWICKSHIRE STRIKE. ,
[Commurn CAI ED ;]

CANON GIRDLESTOICE has. fallen into the
same mistake which vitiated the arguments of
the Saturday Review with reference to the
strike of the Newcastle mechanics. Ile bids
the labourers of Warwickshire consider the
condition of the labourers of Devonshire, and,
in view of the greater hardships endured by
the latter, accept their own lot with thankful-
ness; yes, even spare something out of their
abundance to relieve the needs of their
southern brethren.
Now the doctrine that men should contrast
themselves, not with those above, but with
those below them, is true and wholesome
teaching for persons who possess any share of
the luxuries and superfluities of life; but ad..;
dressed to those who have not yet risen above
the possession of the barest necessaries, and
hold even these at the cost of severe and
exhausting toil, it is as insulting as it is
false.

Thankfulness is a state of the soul produced
by the contemplation of undeserved blessings;
and the man who works from Monday morning
to Saturday night, in return for a pittance
which barely suffices to keep him and his in
the present, and affords no prospect of any
provision for the future, is not likely to deem
that he receives more than his deserts, as to
feel called upon to be grateful to buy one.
Contentment may be a Christian virtue, but
it may also be a most unmanly weakness,
the child of ignorance, cowardice, or despair.
The poor man, brutalised by want, needs to
look up that he may learn what are the condi-
tions of existence under which decency, moral-
ity, sobriety, independence of spirit, and
culture of mind are possible; and the ministers
of Him who came to call all men to a better
life, if they know anything of the intimate
connection which GOD has established, betwixt
body and spirit, should never cease to repeat
the tender invitation of their Master—" Friend,
come up higher."
As for the proposal that the labourers of
Warwiokshire should contribute towards the
support of their brethren in Devonshire, its
author would seem to have been studying the
story of the widow who cast her two mites
into the treasury, and to have discovered in
the praise which CIIRIST bestowed upon her
deed, ground for supposing that He intended
to sanction a general transfer of the burdens
of the rich to the shoulders of the poor,
exonerating the former from bearing their
share of the public burdens, on the plea that
under no Circumstances can the sacrifices made
by them equal in cost the sacrifices made
by the latter: a reading of the passage which
exceeds the licence of interpretation accorded
even to official exponents of the Scriptures.
It is firm, quite true, that the condition of
the Devonshire labourers demands im-
provement ; but are the Warwickshire
labourers the right persons to improve it ?
Do fifteen shillings a week, assuming that
he earns this sum, leave so large a margin at
a man's disposal, after he has done fairly by
his own family, as to warrant him in supple-
menting the wages paid by Devonshire
farmers, or in relieving the pressure of Devon-
shire rates ?

Callon GIRDLESTONE may rest assured that
the men of Warwickshire are not ignorant of
the fad that the men of Devonshire are worse
off than they, though they differ from him in
their view of the source from which their
fellows poverty is to be remedied, and the
part they are to play in. removing it; and their

strike assumes in their eyes a nobler aspect
from the reflection that their victory, if they
prove victorious, will profit those who are too
weak as yet to fight their own battles. Nay
more; if learning no lesson from the defeat of
the landowners and farmers of the Midland
counties, the landowners and farmers of the
south continue to flatter themselves that they
shall always ba allowed to get labour cheap,
at the expense of the ratepayers or the chari-
table, the labourers of Warwickshire out of
their enhanced earnings, will gladly aid their
southern brethren in a struggle to secure such
remuneration for their toil as shall thence-
forward raise them above the humiliating
necessity of looking elsewhere than to their
own-earnings for support.
If genuine compassion for the miserable
condition of the southern labourer prompted
the CANON'S letter of advice, he may take to
heart the comforting assurance that the road
on which the Warwickshire labourers have
entered, is more likely to lead to the realisation
of his good wishes on behalf of his clients, than
the course which he recommends; if other
feelings guided his pen, it is perhaps not
altogether useless to prove to him that it is
not difficult to detect, under his specious pro-
posal, a new rate in aid of wages, to be levied
on those who can least afford to pay it, for the
benefit of those who have the least claim to
receive it, to the detriment of the very persons
whom it would appear to relieve.

articles.title: TERRIBLE EARTHQUAKES,
articles.text:
TERRIBLE EARTHQUAKES,

Despatches dated San Francisco, March 29,
state that advices from the volcanic country
north of the Mojare river show that an earth-
quake had been felt there with terrible force.
At Lone Pine 23 people were killed. The
shocks were felt at intervals for 30 hours,
creating immense consternation. Fifty houses
were wholly demolished, and the town is in
ruins. Despatches from Genoa, Nevada, dated
March 28, say that Camp Independence, Ingo
County, California, is- in complete ruins, the
earthquake (March 26) having been most
severe in that region. Not a single abode
or brick building is standing from Bishop's
Creek to Independence. Fears are entertained
for other mining camps further south in the
sierras. Stage passengers report several
fissures miles in length, and 50 to 200 feet
wide and 20 feet deep, opened along the
eastern base of the Sierra Nevada near Big
Pine Camp. At other places in the vicinity
the ground is heaved up in great ridges.
Large springs have stopped running, and
others have broken out. Many people at
Independence were hurt, but no lives were
lost. The shock was probably more severely
felt south-eastward towards Arizona, in the
desert country, which has hardly any popu-
lation.

EMIGRATION FOR 1872.
To the Editor of the BEE-EftvE.

Sra,—The Canadian Government is most
judiciously putting forth extra efforts to attract
emigrants. The Ontario Government (Canada
West) besides offering 100 acres of land free to
all over 18, is cutting down 5 acres of timber
and erecting a shanty (wooden house), to be
repaid by yearly instalments by settlers on the
lots. This year after voting 80,000 dollars,
they probably will grant to each adult settling
in Ontario for three months, a bonus of six
dollars (255.), and something for each child.
This will act very favourably for settlers or
friends advancing monies to carry relatives or
poor people from the Old Country.
The Dominion Government gives free rail-
way passes up country from Quebec to bona
fide emigrants. Office for enquiries, 6, Adam-
street, Adelphi, Strand.—W. Dixon, Esq .
Commissioner.
The New Zealand Government has issued a
very inviting prospectus. Married couples
with or without three children under 12 (other
children can be paid for), being navvies, gene-
ral farm labourers, ploughmen, gardeners,
shepherds, and a few country mechanics, have
passages granted as follows :—on payment of
£l, or £2, or £3, or £4 per adult, with a pro-
mise to pay :£B, or £6, or £4, or £2 respec-
tively; or a full payment of £5 each adult—
and £4 each unmarried man, with a promise
to pay £8; and Free to unmarried females
from 15 to 35 years, promising to pay £5.
This is an admirable opportumty—that is,
for only .{:2 a man, wife, and three children
can emigrate to New Zealand, one of the best
of our colonies. Office, 7, Westminster Cham-
bers, Viotoria-street, Westminster, London.
Victoria (Australia) has injudiciously ceased
helping emigrants. Queensland (Australia)
aids general labourers, &e. ,Office, 32, Charing
Cross, London.
The Direction of Her Majesty's Commis-
sioners is 7, Park-street, Westminster, London,
who give reliable information respecting all
the British Colonies. (N.B.—Enolose a stamped
and directed envelope in making enquiries at
any office.)
Emigration clubs with weekly payments are
being established in Many places. Our Clerk-
cumin club and society has assisted 2,330
persons. The majority, in Canada, are doing
well—work is abundant there. As the season
has begun and applications are numerous, sub-
scriptions are greatly needed to help poor
people wishing to emigrate to our British
Colonies. Who will help P—l remain Sir, yours
obediently,

A. STYLEMAN HERRING,
Incumbent and Chairman.

WHAT SHALL WE GET FOR 'OUR
SCHOOL FEES?
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
my previous communication I
placed before your readers statistics, from the
Government 131ne Book for 1869, which show,
by taking ago with results, that the National,
or Church Schools, are not inferior to the British
or Nonconformist Schools in secular know-
ledge. Dr. W. C. Bennett must therefore seek
elsewhere for reasons why the former should
be suppressed, and the latter established
against the wishes of those who will be called
upon to bear the greater portion of the burden.
, But, in discussing the relative merits of the
two classes of schools, other facts must be
borne in mind; two of these facts I now beg
permission to mention.
First, then, it should not be forgotten that
the said State-aided National Schools are
scattered over the face of the whole country,
while the state-aided Nonconformist Schools
are confined to the more favourable localites.
It would be unreasonable to expect, from the
national children in the wilds of Cumberland,
results as high as those produced. by the
British children at Greenwich. And yet we
have seen that the average results are as high
in the former as in the latter. Hence we may fairly
conclude that, all other things being equal, the
National is superior to the British sohool in
secular instruction.
In the second place it is well known that in
Church schools a vast deal of time is spent in
the acquisition of religious knowledge; that
the managers regard, this subject as of para-
mount importance. I think, then, it will be
readily conceded that the National are supe-
rior to the British schools in religious instruo-
Con. Therefore, without pursuing this sub-
ject further, I think I have shown conclusively
that the education given in the schools which Dr.
Bennett stigmatises as "delusions are snares,"
is superior to the education given in those
schools for which he has not a single word of
hostile criticism.
What, then, shall we get for our school
fee s? To this question I am now in a position
to make the following reply :—ln Church of

England schools you will get better secular
instruction than in the Nonconformist_ (!)r

future Board) schools, and at about half the
cost. In addition you may obtain severe
religious instruction, for which you will be
called upon to pay nothing whatever.
As regards the requirements of Standard
VI., many of your readers have no doubt
passed it, and therefore know it is not so easy
as appears.
What Swiss children know at twelve, I am
not in a position to say. Blessed as they are
with compulsory laws, they certainly ought to
know more than our own; but Dr. Bennett
fails to show that they do; The long extracts
before me are not to the point at all, for they
show only what is attempted in the crack
schools visited by Mr. Dixon, and not what is
accomplished over the whole country.
By the way, does Mr. Hepworth Dixon
mean to say that the Swiss are not taught
"the use of the hyphen, dot, and dash" till
they are ten years of age ?•
Dr. Bennett , must have his fling at "our
parsons," but I would inform him that our
parsons" have been the means of educating
more than 90 per cent. of the children of
woiking men, and that, had it not been for
them' these children would most probably
have been educated for no "state of life" at

all.
Allow me, Sir, to conclude this corre-
spondence by asking why so few working
men seek seats on school boards? Most of
them have passed through our schools, and
therefore ought to know the requirements of
the future better than those who passed their
time in more pretentious seminaries or
academies.—l am, Sir, yours faithfully,
J. BROWN.

LANDLORDS AND FARMERS.
To the Editor of the BEE-FlivE.

Sin,—ln reply to Mr. Lloyd Jones' observa-
tions, would you allow me space to remark
that a landed proprietor is not primarily
answerable for the wages his tenants pay to

their labourers.
Rents are low enough to admit of much
higher wages being paid.
In many instances rents do not cover interest
of money on improvements, such as farm-house
and buildings, drainage, farm-roads, itc., &e.
An Australian or Canadian colonist would
be only too happy to pay rent if he could get
such works executed for him.
Supposing a capitalist were to forsake cotton-
spinning for agriculture, bow would he sot to
work?
Reclaim 5,000 acres of land; divide it into five
'portions of 1,000 acres; appoint a manager to
each portion, and exercise a general superin-
tendence himself over the whole property.
He would in fact carry the factory system
into the farm, and would never think of
trusting his property to an intermediate agent
such as is a farmer.
Lord Derby has recently said that if land
were properly tilled the produce would be
doubled, and if so, food would become much
cheaper for all of us.
Farmers as a body have not the amount of
capital necessary to cultivate the land they
occupy. To cultivate land thoroughly you
must own it yourself, and 5,000 acres would
absorb a capital of about £250,000.
*Under such circumstances, the capitalist
could no doubt afford to pay the agricultural
labourer £1 per week wages.—l am, your
obedient servant,

G. W. FIELD

To the Editor of the BEE-lIIvE.
Sin,—ln your issue of April 6th, in an
article on " Landlords and Farmers," Mr.
Lloyd Jones, in advocating an increase in
the wages of agricultural labourers, amongst
other things, says, it is folly to say the
farmers cannot afford it. They must afford
it; and if present prices will not pay
when they give the higher wages, they must
ask more for their produce. Now, as an
old reader of the BEE-HIVE, and having great
confidence in Mr. Jones as a working-man's
leader and friend, I would ask him and the
readers of your valuable paper the following
questions :—By raising the price of labour, do
we also raise the price of the article which that
labour produces? I mean, does the cost of
production regulate the price of articles? If
so, and we shorten the hours of labour, has it
the same effect? Is money of less value than it
was thirty years ago? Are trades' unions, under
their present management, the best means to
elevate the working classes? Mr. Jones says
ignorance is the curse of God, and I have no
' other object in writing this than seeking infer
mation. I cannot agree with Mr. Jones in
everything he advances. It does, and ever has
appeared to me, that the working classes are
info better position now than they were thirty
years ago. I have no reference to politics
whatever.
I can live, with my family, for ss. a week
loss in a small agricultural town than in a
Lancashire or Yorkshire manufacturing town;
and why? Because the labour which produces
everything in an agricultural county is much
cheaper.
Employers will have the same profits
capitalists the same surplus, with no less

luxurious and. extravagant living. Then' if
we receive a greater price for our labour, the
only thing is, we have more to spend. to buy
the same article. lam well aware if one trade,
or branch of any trade, has a union, the others
must follow, and. I agree with the farm
labourers, and shall assist them so far as I am
able. But if the farmers raise the price of
their produce, according to you, Mr. Editor,
and. at present out of 125., 9s. 4th is taken
for flour and bread alone, what is the use
of higher wages, if out of 165., 13s. ,4d.
is taken for the same? By inserting this you
will oblige, and your readers may be able to
instruct—Yours, &e.,

NON-UNIONIST.

POLYNESIAN LABOUR TRAFFIC.
To the Editor of the BEE-RIVE.

Sin,—l have read the BEE-HIVE for
the last three months without noticin,/ a
single word about the Polynesian Labour Traffic.
Your able and truthful articles on China show
that you feel as honest men ought to feel
about these matters. Let me, therefore, ask
you to tell working men something about this
abominable reproduction of the Slave Trade in
several of its worst forms. Tell them about
Bishop Pattesou's death, and the visits of the
sham missionary ship, which are directly
answerable for that death. Recommend to
them a little pamphlet lately published at
Leeds, "The Polynesian Slave Trade, its
character and tendencies, with reasons for its
total and immediate prohibition." There is
great ignorance about the matter, at leas
among the working men with whom I have
to do. Several, when I spoke of Bishop
Patteson, said. "Oh, you mean that poor man
they put to death last year in Paris." Your
London mechanics of course know better than
that; but still the matter is one on which
too much light cannot be thrown. As the
Saturday Review, some little time ago, con-
fessed, regulation is impossible; prohibition
is what we want, unless the islands are to
be speedily depopulated; and. prohibition we
shall not get unless pressure is put on the
Home Government.
To me even the blowing from guns of the
adherents of a new Indian sect is less heinous

than the traffic carried on in the South Seas by
scoundrels far worse than the pirates whom
Rajah Brooke put down.
Let the working men of England do as
Leeds, Oxford, &AL, have done—send up a
strong representation to Parliament, in behalf
of the poor helpless Polynesians. They are a
long way off, but England's arm ought to be
long enough to reach them.—l am, &a., -
HENRY STUART FAG IN.
St. Just Vicarage, Penzance.

CHRISTIANITY WAS THE SEED OF
CIVILISATION.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
Sin,—Christianity was the seed of civilisa-
tion; and civilisation is the fruit of that seed.
Ex. gr. Before an Emigrant can reap in the
wilderness he must sow; and era he can sow
he must search for seed. And when he has
found and collected seed, he has need to
examine and sift it, as well as to plant it in
order to prove it; and afterwards he has need
to replant the best of the seeds thus obtained
in beds alongside of one another, in order that
their relative qualities or virtues may com-
mingle and be imparted to the seed resulting
from this union, so that he may obtain in one
perfect seed all the qualities which the others
only had possessed collectively in an unde-
veloped, form. And then, with this perfect
seed, he is as able to cover the land with fine
golden waves of corn, as the waters cover the
sea. _ _

Ana In Ike manner Christianity (i.e. the
----
character of Christ), as a seed, was the em-
bodiment or personation in one individual of
all the good qualities and virtues of civilised
individuals collectively. And after this holy
and divine character of Christ had been thus
produoed and manifested as the representative
heir of all the prophets, it was, and is the aim
of all who would educate and civilise
humanity (as it was the mission of Christ) to
reconcile all men to bring themselves to be at
one with the character and conduct of Jesus
Christ, in order that Christ's life and cha-
racter, as a seed, might bear fruit by leaven-
ing, regenerating, and oivilising humanity
individually, until the whole world became
Christian, i.e., Christ-like, and in the image of
God, wherein the Scriptures assert man was
created.
But the great adversaries to the successful
attainment of this civilising mission of
Christ's, were the proud priests and Pharisees,
who, at Jerusalem, incited the people to
destroy (Matt. xxvii. 20) Jesus, in order to
save the theocratic authority and power of
, the Church they had established from being
destroyed (John xi. 48; Mark xii. 7). And
their proud successors abroad and at home,
in order to preserve and continue the
infallible authority and supreme power
of the several Churches, which they
have re-established for the glory of them-
selves as gods, to receive confessions, and, as
saviours, to deliver their worshippers from
from hell through belief in their dogmas, con-
tinue to the present day to incite the people
to persecute and despise as blasphemous

---
heretics and infidel sceptics, all those whore-
fuse to abnegate their reason, and profess
belief in their stereotyped creeds, evil doc-
trines, and mystical sacrifices. And thus, by
their evil traditions, the modern Pharisees are
proved to be as great adversaries to the suc-
cess of Cheist's civilising mission as their pre,
decessors, the ancient Pharisees were
who murdered Jesus; and therefore the
work of Christ, and the glory of God, require
their disestablishment, for the civilising and
exalting of suffering humanity, because they
have blasphemously slandered God's name by
their evil doctrine of atonement; proudly
usurped God's power in their claims to infalli-
ble authority, and. their exercise of supreme
power; and lastly, because they obstinately
refuse to reform their evil doctrines which
make the Word of God in the S criptures of
none effect. Than (in the spirit of Daniel),
"People of England, are ye such fools that,
without examination or knowledge of the
truth, ye would suffer your God to be accused
falsely of having required the innocent blood
of Jesus to be shed ?" See "History of
Susanna" in the Apocryplut, verse 48.—Yours,
&c.
Potersharo, S.W.

T. G. HEADLEY.

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS, To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
articles.text:
THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS,
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

SIR,—Mr. Seeley, M.P., has set an excellent
example in so promptly directing his tenants
to advance their farm labourers 3s. a week, 2s,
of which he will allow by way of reduction of
rent. If this or some similar course is at once
taken in any district, the evils incident to a
struggle between class and class will be
averted, and possibly the Agricultural Trades'
Union will not yet take root, and I, for one,
shall be right glad of it, Notwithstanding
this, however, after twelve years of special op-
portunities of watching these combinations of
the wage-receiving class in various branches
of mechanical industry, I am of opinion that
much credit is due to Mr. George Potter, and
other temperate leaders, for the skill and
judgment they have almost invariably shown
in the difficult task of general management
and regulation of the affairs of the combined
workmen. Their success in regard to the ad-
vances in wages is undoubted. Had employers
been less selfish, more considerate in little
things to their people, and willing to do to
others as they would have others do to them,
the sting would have been taken out of the
men of action who cry strike. I feel convinced
by my own experience, and by observation of
other establishments, that where masters
in any 'business take a kindly interest in
their men (too seldom, alas!) the men see it
and feel it, and trades unions cannot make
way. As a weapon of defence against the
tyranny of capital and might, trades unions
are invaluable; so I heartily trust that the
down-trodden agricultural labourer, who has
at last combined in Warwickshire, will neither
be bribed nor intimidated into giving up his
union. " Union is strength." To aid him in his
struggle, I have already paid my first con-
tribution, and I implore all symip.thisers
with the English serf tr Hind, as he Is called,
to help liberally, and help Now in this first
effort to break up the stiff clay farrows of
Peasant ignorance and submission to the Farmer
and Landowner, I will not trespass on your
space farther than to say that I have arranged
for the labourers on my land at once to have the
same addition to their weekly wage as that
given by Mr. Seeley to his men • also milk
from the farm for their young children at abciiit
cost price.—l am, &e.,
A Minimum IND LANDOWNER.

Regimental schools have now been com.
pletely organised throughout France, and

Fesonted a joint address of confidence to M.

articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

A labourer named Kettle and his second
wife, to whom he has lately been married,
have been arrested at Great Bromley, in
Essex, on a charge of murdering by poison the
male prisoner's first wife. The woman's death
took place in October, and the Indy has been
exhumed by order of the Home Secretary.
On an analysis being made of the viscera by
Professor Stevenson, of Guy's Hospital, it is
understood that a large quantity of arsenic
was discovered, On Saturday the prisoners
were brought before a county magistrate, and
remanded for a week.

---
The alleged robbery of Cape diamonds was
again before the sitting magistrate at Guild-
hall on Saturday, when, as there was no
further evidence against the prisoner, who had
called himself the Count von Eissenberg, he
was discharged.

An action was tried at the Bristol Assizes
on Saturday, in which the Mayor of Exeter
claimed damages from the publisher of the
Times for libel. It consisted of a letter, in
which "a West Countryman," referring to a
riot at a Permissive Bill meeting at Exeter,
charged the plaintiff with conduct unbecoming
the position of chief magistrate of the city.
It was contended for the defence that the state-
ments complained of were true, and that no
imputation upon the Mayor was intended.
The jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff—
damages, ten guineas.

At the Leeds Assizes, on Saturday, a young
lady named Gill, 23 years of age, sought to
recover compensation for breach of promise
of marriage' the defendant being -a farmer six
years older than herself. The ,peculiarity in
the case was that two promises to marry had
been made, neither of which had been ful-
filled. The jury gave the plaintiff X5OO
damages.

A petition of Dr. Lankester, one of the
coroners for Middlesex, came before Mr.
Registrar Pepys on Saturday, praying for a
liquidation of his debts. A receiver to the
estate has been appointed.

Mr. Justice Keogh resumed the hearing of
the Galway election inquiry on Saturday, when
additional evidence was taken showing the
violence of the mob on the day of the polling.
Amongst the witnesses was Sir Arthur Guin-
ness, who lately represented the city of Dub-
lin in the Conservative interest.

In the United States House of Representa-
tive, a Bill has been passed allotting a sum
of 190,000 dollars to the officers and crew of
the Kearsage for the destruction of the
Alabama. The engagement between the two
vessels took place, it will be recollected, in the
English Channel near Cherbourg as far back
as the I9th June, 1864.

According to an announcement in the French
Journal Officio!, M. niers will receive visi-
tors on certain fixed days at the Elyse° Palace,
in Paris, but will not leave his official resi-
donee at Versailles. A Paris correspondent
says that M. Thiers makes no secret of his
desire to be a great deal among his "consti-
tuents, friends, and follow-citizens" in the
capital during the present recess.

A lecture on the Papal Syllabus has been
delivered by the Abbe Junqua at Bordeaux.
1,200 persons are said to have been present,
including several priests.

In the Calcutta Legislative Council on
Saturday, the India Budget. was introduced.
For the financial year 1870-1871 there is a
surplus of .1,482,990, and the Estimates for
1872-73 show a surplus of £237,000. The
Income-tax for 1872-73 is to be one per cent.,
all incomes under 1,000 rupees to be exempted.
No loans on account of public works are to be
contracted, the funds in hand being sufficient.

A telegram from Madrid states that the
Spanish Government, according to its own
representations, has obtained a majority of
100. Another account says the majority is
estimated at 110. The capital remains tran-
quil, but disturbances have taken place in the
provinces. At Cordova, two of the polling
clerks and a man who was assisting the
police had been wounded, the ballot-boxes
were broken, and the electoral lists taken
away. At Santiago a priest came to the
voting.place with a revolver in his hand, and
caused considerable alarm. In Madrid the
Opposition has obtained 32,287 votes, and the
Ministerialists 9,230. Senor Sagasta is now
completely restored to health.

• On the 26th March an attempt was made
by twelve conspirators at Yeddo to assassinate
the Mikado of Japan, but it failed. Two of
the conspirators were captured; the rest
escaped. It is thought that the attempt is
part of the old widespread conspiracy against
the Mikado. The Japanese autthorities are
uneasy, and have warned foreigners not to go
beyond the city limits.

The Duke of Edinburgh on Monday pre-
sided over the annual meeting of the Royal
National Lifeboat Institution, which was held
at the Mansion House, and, in the course of
his Opening address, his Royal Highness spoke
in the highest terms of the value of this
admirable organisation. Admiral Sir •G.
Sartoris, Admiral Sir John Hay, the Lord
Mayor,- Sheriff. Sir John Bennett, Sir James
Elphinstone, and Lord Garlies were amongst
the speakers.

A numerous deputation on Monday pro-
seated a memorial to Mr. Stansfeld, praying
for an alteration in some of the details of the
Public Health Bill, and suggesting the appoint-
ment of one central authority, which should
have the control of sanitary matters. The
right hon. gentleman promised to consider the
points brought before him.

The funeral of the late Mr. John Peel, M.P.
for Tamworth, took place on Monday, at Mid-
dleton Church, a large number of the tenantry
and of the late member's constituents joining
in the procession. For the seat rendered
vacant through his death, Mr. T. W. Evans,
who represented South Derbyshire in the
Liberal interest from 1837 to 1868, has been
invited to become a candidate, but has de-
clined to come forward.

At the Bridgenorth Steeplechases on Mon-
day, the Grand Stand suddenly gave way,
and about 150 of its occupants were more or
less hurt.

An application was made on Monday to
Mr. Registrar Hazlitt on the part of Moritz
Heymann, a bankrupt, to rescind a warrant
of arrest granted on the ground that he was
about to depart the Kingdom. His Honour
consented to suspend the operation of the
warrant for a week.

On the 7th inst. the Dromedary, with
Government stores, ran ashore at the back of
the Isle of Wight..

On the 4th inst. the Prince and Princess of
Wales were entertained at a grand dinner at
the Quirinal.

A. collection of personal jewellery belonging
to the Empress of the French, consisting of
some beautiful brooches, bracelets, necklaces,
and fans, is at present offered for sale at
Amsterdam.

Sir Hercules Robinson, K.C.M.G., will
leave England shortly, by the French
marine service, for Sydney, New South Wales,

An official report on Jamaica, which is
shortly to be laid before Parliament, shows
that the condition of the island has greatly
improved since the introduction of the new
constitution four years ago. The import dues
have been reduced, and the tonnage dues upon
trading vessels abolished. There has been a
surplus of £30,000 for 1870-71, though the
reduction of taxation amounted to £.11,000
during the previous two years. The public
debt has been reduced by £227,800, and will
be entirely paid off in 27 years. Much de-
moralisation was form6rly caused by the
squatting system. The uncultivated 'awls of
the colony have now been taken possession of
by the Government where no owner is appa-
rent, in virtue of a bill passed by the Legis-
lative Council, and leases are granted. The
result is that the squatters get a good lease at
a fair rent in exchange for their previously
precarious tenure. Public works are being
carried out at considerable cost, and efforts
aro making to acclimatise valuable trees and
plants hitherto unknown in the island. While
the material condition of Jamaica is thus
satisfactory its mental condition is fall of
promise. Schools are increasing, and, their
standard of instruction has risen considerably
since 1865.

A memorial has been presented by the
Manchester Chamber of Commerce to Earl
Granville in reference to the French Treaty.
The memorialists renew their protest against the
slightest movement of retrograde character,
and express their regret that, after twelve
years' experience of the operation of the treaty,
the French Government should return to a
system of protection, which will inevitably
cripple their commerce and check its further
expansion. The memorialists further express
a hope that Earl Granville will not be a party
to the adoption of retaliatory legislation on
French imports, or to the imposition of export
duties.

been chosen referee, they effected an even
start, Ridgway having the worst station; he
soon, however, drew in front, and won event-
ually by four lengths; the race after half a
mile being virtually over, and the losers out-
inatehed in strength and style.

At the seventy-eighth quarterly meeting
of the Conservative Land Society, held on
Tuesday, at the Norfolk-street Offices, Viscount
lianelagla in the chair, the receipts for the
quarter ending Lady-day last were declared to
be £26,215 16$. 6d., and the grand totals to
the same date, £1,770,428 10s. 9d. The total
withdrawaiS were £466,803 6s. 10d. The
number of the last share issued was 37,194.
The reserve fund (exclusive of office preniiBoB)
&o.) amounts to £10,600. The rate at interest
remains at 6 per cent. per annum on shares,
and 4 per cent. per annum on deposits.

The Melbourne Herold of the 14th
February contains the following :—" In one of
the Government offices, Melbourne, is a clerk,
who has in his possession a ring bearing the.
Tichborne coat of arms, and on the inside the
name of Roger Tiehborne's sister engraved.
The ring was purchased for a trifle from a
pawnbroker, who disposed of it at a low
figure on account of a difficulty being ex-
perienced in selling it, owing to the crest.
This ring was seen by our informant in the
possession of the individual referred to. The
question is,how did this ring get into the pos-
session of the pawnbroker ? Something impor-
tant to the issue of the trial might hang on
that."

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

• HOUSE OF COMM ONS.—MONDA.Y.
THE BALLOT BILL
The House went into Committee on the
Ballot Bill. Clause 2, which prescribes the
, manner in -which the poll shall be taken was
commenced, and on the first line of it more
than two hours was occupied in discussing a
variety of suggestions for extending the hours
of polling.
Sir C. Dilke moved the insertion of words
fixing the hours from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., and
Mr. Forster, on the part of the Government,
declined to accept the amendment, on the
ground that to carry on the polling after dark
would favour personation and disturbance.
Mr. Torrens re,torted that it was inconsistent
in the Government to apprehend darkness,
because the Ballot itself was secret, and the
proposal was supported by Mr. Rathbone, Mr.
Dixon, Mr. Goldsmid, Mr. C. Bentinck, and
Mr. T. Hughes, and opposed by Mr. Hardy,
Mr. Powell, Mr. Hope, Mr. Kay-Shuttleworth,
and others.
Sir J. Elphinstone was of opinion that to
open the poll at 6 a.m. would be more con-
Venient for the working men, and moved an
amendment to that effect.
Mr, Whitbread suggested that sunset should
be the limit of the polling hours, and Mr.
Forster, after some consideration, accepted
this., and promised on the report to bring up
words carrying out the idea that the poll shall
close as nearly as possible at sunset, bid never
before 4 or later than 8 p.m.
Sir James Elphinstone and Lord Elcho
pointed out the discrepancies which would
follow from the different geographical position
of different constituencies, and strong objec-
tions to the " slifling scale" were urged by
other members. After a long conversation, in
which very discordant opinions were ex-
pressed, three divisions were taken,
in the first place Sir John Elphinstone's
motion to begin at 6 a.m. was negatived by
242 to 66.
Mr. Collins then proposed that the poll
shall close at 5 p.m., and on a Division the
hour of 6 p.m. proposed by Sir C. Dilke was
struck out of his amendment by 106 to 98,
but the Committee refused by 157 to 93 to
fill up the blank with 5 p.m.
Mr. Monk then proposed 6 p.m., but ulti-
mately Sir Charles Bilk() relinquished alto-
gether his attempt to extend the hours, and
left the question in the hands of the Govern-
taent to move a sliding scale en the Report,
Mr. Herman wound up the conversation
by expressing a hope that when Mr. Forster
had made up his mind to another proposal he
would stand by it.
After this Mr: 4. Lowther again submitted
.to the Committee• an elaborate scheme for
taking the poll by voting papers, which Mr.
Forster again met by the objection that it would
defeat the intention of the Bill, and that the
House, having passed the second reading,
would stultify itself by accepting this scheme.
On a division the arnendinent was negatived
by Si to 36.
Mr. C. Bentinok then moved the first of a
series of amendments designed to alter the form
of the Ballot, so as to make it a more open
Ballot, which after a short discussion, was
rejected by 14,3 to 00;• and a second •amend-
ment of the same series was negatived by 199
to 104.
Lord Mahon then renewed the proposal to
provide for a scrutiny by requiring that each
Ballot paper shall bear a number correspond-
ing to the number on the counterfoil from
which it is torn. He gave way, however, in
favour of Mr. Gregory, who proposed to obtain
the same end by requiring the Returning
Officer to inscribe on the Ballot paper the
voter's number on the register. This was
debated for some time, the arguments in favour
of a scrutiny, and the impossibility of prevent-
ing personation without it, being urged by
Colonel Bartelot, Mr. Hunt, ,Mr. Cross, and
Mr. Collins.
Mi;M'CullaghTorrens also spoke on the same
side from the Liberal benches, protesting
against the notion that Parliament should
legislate for the craven minority, and appealing
to the authority of Mr. Bright.
On the other hand, the Solicitor-General and
,Mr. Forster argued that the absolute secrecy
which is the essence of the Bill .was incon-
eistent with a •scrutiny, and that ample
securities were taken in other ways for the
prevention of personation. .
On a division Mr. Gregory's amendment was
negatived by 166 to 126.
The further progress of the Bill was then
adjourned until Thursday.

ITOUSE COMMONS.—TUEBD SY.
On Tuesday, Colonel Beresford called at-
tention to the unfair and ruinous competition
with which tho mat trade has to contefld. in
consequence of the extensive employment of
convict labour in the manufacture. lie com-
plained also of the application of steam power
in Wakefield Prison to the trade, and of the
prices at which the product of convict labour
is sold, and he moved for a Select Committee
to inquire into the subject.
Mr. KetlllaWay proposed to give a wider
scope to the inquiry by referring to the Com-
mittee the Whole question of Prison Labour in

our gaols. He prefaced an amendment to this
effect by an interesting review of the history
of the industrial system of prison discipline,
which was very much needed as to the most
beneficial form of Prison Labour, and ex-
pressed a hope that it would help to educate
the working classes out of doors as to the
expediency of employing prisoners on indus-
trial labour.
Major Waterhouse and Mr. Akroyd,
justices of Wakefield Prison, vindicated
the system of labour pursued there, and Mr.
Whitwell, Mr. Liddell, and Mr. T. Collins de-
precated the appointment of a committee, as
seeming to throw a doubt on the value of
prison labour.
Mr. Locke reiterated Colonel Beresford's
complaint that the prison authorities under-
sold the regular trade, and Mr. Morley, though
favourable to remunerative labour in our pri-
sons, thought that the 3,000 workpeople who
complained of a grievance ought to have it
inquired into.
Ali% J. G. Talbot was in favour of an inquiry
into our whole system of penal discipline.
Mr. Bruce, speaking of the convict prisons
under the control of the Government, said
there were only two in which mat-making was
practised, and explained that the genet al rule
in large prisons was to teach as many trades
as possible. No doubt there was a run on mat-
making, and almost necessarily, because it
was easily 'taught to prisoners confined on the
separate system, and for short periods; but he
denied that there was any desire to undersell,
or that there was any reality in the grievance.
The limited inquiry, therefore, asked by
Colonel Beresford was uunecessarY ; and he
objected also to the larger inquiry of Mr. Ken-
naway, contending, with copious extracts from
the criminal statistics, that crime has dimin-
ished, and that there is no need for apprehend-
ing the failure of our system of prison disci-
pline.
The motion and amendment were then
withdrawn.
Mr. W. Fowler next moved a resolution
condemning the present state of the law of
entail and strict settlement of land as a dis-
couragement to the investment of capital in
the development of agriculture. In support of
it he drew first a forcible picture of the position
of the limited owner or tenant for life, and this
led him into alengthy digression on the wretched
provision of agricultural cottages, and the
general condition of the agricultural labourer.
All the hardships and miseries endured by this
()lass he traced to the land laws, which, by
checking the flow of' capital on to the land,
prevented high agriculture- and kept down
wages. Land, he complained, was too much
regarded in this country as a luxury or as an
instrument of social and political power, and
he desired to see it more sought fOr by those
who would make money out of it. Deprecating
all idea of breaking up largo estates or of in-
troducing tho French system, he was in favour
of having a much larger number of persons
interested in the land, and this be thought
would be brought about by removing all
trammels on the devolution of land, allowing
it perfect freedom, and by leaving each genera-
tion to take care of itself. Mr. Fowler also
touched on other evils of the present system,
such as the temptations to extravagance on
the part of the young heir, the drawbacks to
granting leases, and also on the cumbrous
processes of transferring land.
Mr. Brand, in seconding the motion, insisted
that but for life tenancies the land might be
made to yield considerably more than at pre-
sent, and pleaded strongly for a reform in our
Land Laws, which would give landlords full
liberty to deal with their estates.
Mr. Read doubted whether entails were so
much of a discouragement to the development
of agriculture, and pointed to other and more
powerful drawbacks to the profitable invest-
ment of capital in the land, such as eopyhold
tenures, heavy Rates, the want of security for
improvements, the Game Laws, the Malt Tax,
the law and the lawyers, and, above all, the
"family lawyer," whom he held in the greatest
horror. The greater part of Mr. Fowler's
remarks on the condition of the agricultural
labourer, he held, had. nothing to do with the
subject; and as to the cottages, much worse
sights might be seen in towns.
Mr. Wren-Hoskyns dwelt on the impedi-
ments to the transfer of land, and traced a
close connexion between the present tenure of
land and the condition of the agricultural
labourer. He was favourable to entails for
existing lives, but would abolish the power of
tying up for 21. years after.
Mar. Gregory denied that entails were the
cause of the delays, expense, and hindrances to
agriculture complained of, and showed that
tenants for life had much larger powers than
Mr. Fowler represented.
Mr. Dent and Lord F. Cavendish spoke in
favour of a reform of the _Land Laws, which
would attract more capital to the land and thus
raise wages; while Sir F. Goldsmid, admitting
sena° drawbacks in the Law of Settlement,
thought its defects had been much exag-
prated, anti certainly could not be charged
with the condition of labourers' cottages, or
with the granting or refusal of leases.
Mr. Disraeli, referring to a case cited by
Mr. Fowler in illustration of his argument
about labourers' cottages, informed him that

the row of cottages in question—the condition
of which it was impossible to condemn too
strongly—belonged to no landlord and to no
estate, They were built some years ago on
the waste by a tradesman from a neighbouring
town—a leading Liberal, by the way—and
they had nothing to do, therefore, with the
Law of Entail. On the general question, Mr.
Disraeli was of opinion that it would require
consideration as a whole, though the time was
not ripe for passing any such resolution as
that before the House; and be repeated his
opinion that the condition of the agricultural
labourer is slowly but surely improving.
.Mr. Gladstone agreed with Mr. Disraeli that
the question had not been sufficiently discussed
for an opinion to be pronounced. upon it, and
while the Government was under pledges to
deal with the Transfer of Land and the Suc-
cession to Intestate Estates they would not be
wise to take on themselves this further ques-
tion of Entails. The abolition of the present
system, in Mr. Gladstone's opinion would not
affect the distribution :of estates in this
country, which depended MOTO on social and
economical causes, taken in connection with
the limited area of the soil. But whenever
the Government came to deal with the question
it would be better that they should not be
fettered by an abstract resolution, and he asked
Mr. Fowler, therefore, not to press his motion.
. Mr. Fowler declined, and suggested to Mr.
Gladstone that if he was not prepared to give
an opinion it was very easy for hini to walk out
without voting.
On a division, the resolution was negatived
by 103 to 81, and the result was greeted with
loud cheers from below the gangway.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEimEsn,tY.
Two petitions, one from 891 inhabitants of
certain parishes in Hampshire, and from 523
of the people of Poole, praying that no public

The Poor Law (Sootland) Bill was the next

The Lord Advocate was not present, but an

The discussion, however, proceeded, and
after an attempt on the part of Mr. Crau.forcl
to reply to the objections urged. against the
Bill, which was immediately suppresseed
because no amendment had been moved, the
second reading was passed. without a division.
Next came the Sunday Trading (Metropolis)
Bill, the second reading of which was moved.
by Mr. 3, G. Talbot, but after a general
discussion it was rejected by a majority
of 29.
The nomination of a select committee for
the Municipal Corporations (Borough Funds)
Bill terminated. the sitting.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tnunsrax.
Earl Granville, in reply to Earl .Stanhope
said he had great pleasure in informing the
noble earl that the French charge (l'affaires
had called upon him and stated that within

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIWRSDAY.
Mr. John Bright was present at the com-
mencement of the sitting, but, as he entered
the House before prayers, there was no de-
monstration on the part of members.
Mr. Dixon moved the rejection of the Wol-
verhampton, Walsall, and Midland Junction
Railway Bill, on the ground that the new line
involved the destruction of Sutton Colefield
Park, which bore the same relation to Bir-
mingham as Epping Forest did to London.
It was proposed to run the line through the
centre of the park, and though it was true that
only sixteen acres out of the 2,400 comprising
the park would be taken by the Company, yet
these sixteen acres formed the most beautiful
and picturesque portion of it.
Mr. Newdegate seconded the motion.
Mr. C. Forstei supported the Bill, denying
that it .would spoil the park, or that the
inhabitants of thitton were opposed to it.
After some remarks, Mr. Dixon withdrew
his motion, on the understanding that the
opponents of the Bill would have a locus stands:
before the House of Lords.
Mr. C. Fortesque, replying to Mr. Kay-
Shuttleworth, said that under the Act of last
session the Board of Trade had appointed an
oflicer to analyse the water supply by the
various Metropolitan water companies, and that
the results of the analyses were not at all
satisfaotory.

APRIL 13, 1872.

LATEST INTELLICI-ENCE.

FRIDAY.
The Directors of the Bank of England
yesterday further advanced the rate of dis-
count to 4 per cent., a measure probably
necessary, owing to the unnecessary pressure
from the public throughout the past week.
The trial of the boy Arthur O'Connor, took
place yesterday at the Central Criminal Court,
when his counsel Mr. Hume Williams, applied
that the prisoner's plea of guilty should be
withdrawn, and that the question of his capa-
city to plead should be submitted to a jury.
This was at first opposed by the Attorney
-
General, on behalf of the Treasury.; but at
length he withdrew his opposition, and the jury
were sworn to try the fitness of the prisoner to
plead. Prisoner's father and mother, Drs.
Luke, Savven, and Smith, gave evidence of the
youth's want of intellect, but the jury at the
close of the evidence, said they were satisfied
prisoner was of sound mind. He was then
called up for judgement, and sentenced to
twelve months; hard labour and to receive
twenty stripes from a birch rod.
Much painful interest continues to be mani-
fested with regard to the murder of Madame
Rid. The body has been removed to Paris.
Application was made to Sir Thomrs Henry%
yesterday, at Bow street, for a warrant for
the apprehension, with a view to the retnoval
to this country under the extradition treaty,
of the woman Marguerite Dimblo,ne, against
whom the verdict of wilful murder was sub-
sequently returned. This was granted, and.
it is understood that Inspectors Druscovitch
and Pay have left England for the Continent,
such information having been received that
gives a fair prospect &at by the time this
report is published the woman will have been
apprehended.
Mr. Luke Bradley, inspector at Copley
Sidings, near Leeds, was knocked down and
killed yesterday morning by an express train
from Leeds to Liverpool. The accident gave
rise to a rumour that a terrible acoident bad.
occurred, and that several passengers had
been killed.
On the application of Mr. Huddleston,
Mr. Baron Cleashy yesterday consented to
postpone the trial of Mr. Edmund Edmunds,
of Newent, for the murder of his wife, until
the next session of the Central Criminal Court,
affidavits being presented of the non-attend-
ance of material witnesses in the case,
amongst whom was Mr. Mathews, brother of
the late Mrs. Edmunds. Mr. Digby Seymour,
Q.C., appeared on behalf of the prosecution.
From Philadelphia we learn that the Cabinet
had, up to the 11th inst. (yesterday), done
nothing with respect to Earl Granville's note.
All action is postponed until after information
has been received of the proceedings at Geneva
on Monday next.
On the 16th inst., memorial services are to
be held all over the United States, and in all
countries that will participate, in honour of
the late Professor Morse. It is desired to
make these services simultaneous with those
appointed to be held in the Hall of the House
of Representatives at Washington on the
evening of the day mentioned.
The Vestry of St. George's, Hanover "
square, at their meeting yesterday, instructed
their clerk to prepare a petition to the House
of Commons praying for the dissolution of the
union between the parishes of St. George
Hanover-square, and St. Margaret's and St!
John's, Westminster, on account of the un-
equal basis on which the united parishes con-
tribute to the union fund.

Mr. John Bright left Roolidale for London
on Tuesday. Though the health of the right
hon. gentleman is much improved, he still
exhibits traces of the illness which has, during
the last two years, laid him aside from public
duty.
A. marriage is, it is reported, on the tapis
between Miss Fox, the daughter of Lady
Holland, and Prince Withengenstein.
Sir Spencer Robinson held a large and
enthusiastic meeting at Tamworth on Tuesday
night. A unanimous vote of confidence was
passed.
At Greenock, on Tuesday, a carter. named.
James Clark, was sentenced to forty days' ini
prisonment for having feloniously used violence
to two carters with a view to make them leave
their employment.
Mr. Rylands will, in Committee of Supply
on the Civil Service Estimates, move to reduce
the charges on account of her Majesty'amissions
,
abroad by the ' undermentioned sums—viz.'
Argentine Republic £1,400;
Greece, £2,000 ;
and Switzerland, 11,300. And to omit the
following items—viz., Secretary of Legation,

' crotary of Lega-
tion, Coburg, £850; Secretary of Legation,
Greece, £500; and Secretary of Legation,
Switzerland, £400;
making a total reduction
of £6,950.
Her Majesty, it is stated, beforo leaving
Baden, forwarded. £5O to the Rev. Dr.
Hawkins, the British chaplain, for
the
charities in connection with his church in that
town. Her Majesty also presented A costly
bracelet to Mrs. Hawkins as a ouvenir of the
Royal visit.

POEM OF OUR PEASANT.
To hardship from his cradle bred,
Our peasant toils from morn till night,
Tutored by his untutored head
To know his left hand from his right;
Content, in ignorance and clay,
To work for eighteen pence a day.*
But when his hard-earned means he'd share
With one who can with care disburse,—
Row they've enough and yet to spare
Within their little canvas pnrse,
That frugal pair alone can say,
Who live on eighteen pence a day.
How Betty and her sturdy mate,
With beans and bacon in the pot,
Can always find a place and plate
For any pilgrim at their cot,
let Betty and her partner say,
Who live on eighteen pence a day.'
how six or seven successive shoots, "
Still growing fast, yet still ungrown,
Are plied with wrappers, bread and boots,—
Involves a secret only known ,
To parents whose united pay
Is found in eighteen pence a day.
But oh! 'tis not so hard to learn,

As age o'ertakes our frugal pair,
How, blind or crippled, the must turn
To seek the dreaded parish fare,
When health and strength have passed away,
And stopped their eighteen pence a day.
How Betty and her aged mate,
Without a friend, without a tome,
Are borne to earth in parish state
And laid within a pauper's tomb,
While living peasants learn the way
Of those 'at eighteen pence a day.
FRANK FOSTER.

According to a Berlin telegram, many
Alsatians have voluntarily enlisted in the
Gorman regiments at Strasburg.

An influential deputation from Belfast and
other places in the:north of Ireland on Wed-
nesday waited upon Mr. Gladstone, and in-
vited. the right bon. gentleman" to a publie
banquet at Belfast. Tho Premier, in accept-
ing the invitation, expressed a hope that Ire-
land would be found in a satisfactory condi-
tion in all respects. He would communicate
with Mr. M'Clure, M.P., regarding the date
at which he expected to be able to visit the
sister island.

The anniversary festivals of Wednesday in-
cluded those of the Newsvendors' Benevolent
and Provident Institution, the British Home
for Incurables, the Railway Guards' Friendly
Society, the Female Orphan Asylum, and the
National Hospital for the Paralysed and the
Epileptic.

A Paris telegram states that acoording to a
formal declaration made by M. Thiers, the
French Government intends to abandon the
present passport system, and will henceforth
merely require the names of travellers at the
frontiers, no visa or fee being demanded. -

The directors of the Manchester Chamber of
Commerce have sent a memorial to Earl Gran-
ville expressing the hope that during the year
to come his lordship will use every effort to
induce the French Government to go forward
in the path of unrestricted freedom of com-
merce; and especially that he will assure the
French Government that he will not be a party
to the adoption of retaliatory legislation on
French imports, or to the imposition of export
duties.

The Guardian gives the following interest-
ing particulars relating to the last hours of
the late Mr. Maurice Mr. Maurice had
been suffering for some weeks from an illness
caused by internal obstruction, and had more
than once been in serious danger. Having
rallied somewhat from the first attacks, he
was removed from Cambridge to London, and
spent his last days at the house of his nieces,
the Misses Sterling, in Bolton-row. Last
Saturday ho was pronounced by his physician
to be better than he had been since his
removal. But on Sunday he was attacked by
pleurisy, and in the evening it became evident
that the vital powers were failing fast. In
the night he requested that his friend, Mr.
Ll. Davies should be sent for to administer
the Holy Communion, but he desired to post-
pone the partaking till his sons, who had been
summened, should be present to join in it.
Wheni Mr. Davies arrived he had already
become unconscious, and he expired peace-
fully a little before seven a.m. Immediately
before the losing of consciousness he seemed
to gather himself together for an effort, and
repeated audibly the words of the Benediction
at the end of the Communion Office, adding
with einphasis—after the words be with you
be with us all.'"
